articles.headline: Tyrese Proctor showcases the Cleveland Cavaliers' true potential beyond the stars
keyFacts: On Saturday night, the depleted Cleveland Cavaliers defeated the Dallas Mavericks 127-117 without their entire starting lineup due to injuries and travel disruptions.
Sophomore guard Tyrese Proctor led the Cavaliers with a triple-double of 24 points, 11 rebounds, and 10 assists during the win.
Head coach Kenny Atkinson will evaluate future team play after bench players demonstrated unexpected impact beyond the star-studded starters.
body: It has been a shaky 2026-27 NBA season for the Cleveland Cavaliers. They have had some good moments, but there are instances when they show that they are not ready for the big moments.

On Saturday night, the Cavaliers had multiple players out citing all kinds of reasons, including injury management and extreme travel disruptions. With the entire starting lineup out, the Cavaliers had to do their best to beat the Dallas Mavericks, and they did with a score of 127-117.
Tyrese Proctor proves the Cavs can be much better this season

The standout player for the Cavaliers on Saturday was sophomore guard Tyrese Proctor. He was fantastic, as he got a triple-double of 24 points, 11 rebounds, and 10 assists in the win over the Mavericks that have Kyrie Irving and Cooper Flagg.

Mario Hezonja chipped in with an uber-efficient game of 22 points on 9-for-12 shooting from the field, rookie Meleek Thomas continued his hot streak with 20 points, and Thomas Bryant got a solid double-double of 10 points and 11 rebounds.

This was a performance that the Cavaliers needed, as they would've gone under .500 again if they had lost. Thankfully, Proctor has proven that the Cavaliers are much better than just their star-studded starting lineup.

"Win at all cost mentality. Just keep fighting. We're down bodies all the time. We’re a really deep team. So, stay hungry, stay ready, and just be ready when your number is called," Proctor said in his post-game interview after a triple-double performance.

Moving forward, head coach Kenny Atkinson will definitely look into how his team will play in the future. The starters are the focal points, but the rest of the team have proven that they can be much more impactful than expected.

articles.headline: Respect? Exposure? Why England's star names are going abroad
keyFacts: An increasing number of England star players, including Harry Kane, Jude Bellingham, and Anthony Gordon, are choosing to play their club football abroad.
Football Association technical director John McDermott stated that playing in Europe provides players with valuable cultural, technical, and physical development benefits.
Anthony Gordon said he believes his football quality and IQ are receiving more recognition since his transfer to Barcelona.
body: - Published
Bayern Munich's Ballon d'Or winner Harry Kane, Real Madrid's Jude Bellingham, Barcelona's Anthony Gordon - three of England's star players, all of whom are playing their club football abroad.

The Premier League is widely regarded as the most competitive league in the world with the greatest financial muscle, but that does not always translate to the biggest individual profiles and, increasingly, star names are looking elsewhere.

Since Cristiano Ronaldo won the Ballon d'Or in 2008, for example, only Rodri in 2024 was playing in England at the time of being crowned the best player in the world. Michael Owen, in 2001, was the last Englishman to do so while in England.

The trend of English players going abroad has gathered pace since a teenage Jadon Sancho signed for Borussia Dortmund in 2017 and that is reflected in this current Three Lions squad - seven of the initial 25 play outside England.

"Jude Bellingham and Harry Kane were decisive for us in the World Cup and I see no reason they won't be in the future," said England boss Thomas Tuchel when talking about his big stars playing outside of their home country.

"It's good that Anthony has stepped up now. He is the third one. There is obviously a relevance to them playing abroad but I don't see that a player who plays in the Premier League cannot step up and be decisive for us."
At the World Cup in the summer and during the last international break, however, it was those three players' goals and assists that proved decisive.
What could the impact be?
Currently there are 43 English players on the Football Association's radar playing their club football in Europe.
The FA's technical director John McDermott believes it is a "huge positive" to have so many players playing across Europe.

"I spoke to a couple of the boys that are playing abroad at the moment," he told BBC Sport. "The exposure they get in those leagues, playing Champions League or European football, where you're not necessarily having to bang out 55 games, but you still have got time to do your weight training and your gym work.

"Often if you're playing in the English competition or in the EFL, where it's 46 games - you know it's game, game, game, which is fantastic - but for some players that opportunity to get the training in-between and to practise developing on technique or other areas, there's benefits to that."
McDermott was previously at Tottenham Hotspur and says that even when he was in club football, he was a "big believer" in players going abroad to "develop character" and "independence".
"I think being in another changing room and learning another language just puts you under the pressure to adapt," he added.

"And I think for any young person that ability not only to become technically, tactically more adept, but also culturally have to pick up something else - it's huge and prevents people from becoming complacent or just getting used to the same old, same old."
Gordon said in the recent international break he feels he gets more respect now he plays for one of Europe's elite sides, compared with when he was at Newcastle.
"I think he's always been respected," McDermott said.

"I remember when Trips (Kieran Trippier) came back, and Trips was a good player, but when he came back from Atletico (Madrid) I noticed he was just maybe tighter technically and noticed there was a change that Kieran came back with.

"So I'm not sure if he's respected more ... but I think you want all of the players - whether they stay in England [or not] - every six months you see this sort of incremental step where they've added something, another dimension to the game.
"That can sometimes come in this country, obviously, playing with different players, being in new competitions, but I think going abroad definitely helps that.
"And I've seen that with Anthony already and some of the other boys. They come back, it's four months since you've seen them and there's another dimension there."

McDermott is keen to make clear that developing in England can still be of a huge benefit and that Jarell Quansah and Jobe Bellingham, two of England's squad who are now playing in Germany, also played in the EFL.
"There's all different ways, I don't think there's this elixir, I don't think there's this magic formula, 'this is the way'," McDermott said.
England reached the semi-finals of the World Cup for just the third time in their history in the summer.
McDermott was asked if he thought now the Three Lions had more players abroad, it could help develop England's style or performance in major tournaments.
"Yeah, possibly. Again don't underestimate if you're playing now in the Champions League at an English club," he said.
"We would like more players in the pipeline. I think at the moment we're on about 26% or 27% English-qualified players playing the Premier League.
"We've got 40 to 50 players playing at Champions League quality and playing in European football, top Premier League clubs, so let's not underestimate our own product."
McDermott says it is clear the impact having players in different countries is having on the squad, but it is then down to the manager to blend the style.
"I think the different cultural experiences they get, the different exposure they get to play in different types of football is fantastic.

"But still, the England manager has got to try and find that singular blend when they come back of the English players, the Spanish players, the German players, the Italian players, it's all sort of an eclectic mix that they're bringing."
People did not respect 'quality and IQ' in England
Gordon has impressed since making his move to Barcelona in the summer with three goals and five assists in 15 appearances in all competitions.
The 25-year-old is regularly lining up with some of the best players in the world, in a front line alongside Lamine Yamal and Raphinha.
The lure of European giants like Real Madrid, Barcelona and Bayern Munich is hard for any player to turn down.
Arsenal's approach for Vinicius Jr this summer was always going to be hard to complete as the famous white shirt and lifestyle in Madrid is, for most players, the pinnacle.
But does moving abroad to one of Europe's top clubs also alter people's perceptions of English players?
"I always felt in England, people respected me because I was fast and I pressed, but they never actually respected the quality and IQ that I play with," Gordon said in a recent interview with ITV.

"Only the players I play with ever seem to notice that. I think now I'm at Barcelona and I play a different style, those qualities are highlighted much more and people are actually starting to take notice that I'm not just quick."

Gordon produced some standout moments in the World Cup, assisting both of Kane's goals in the last-32 win over DR Congo, winning a penalty in England's last-16 win over Mexico and scoring the goal to put England ahead in the semi-final against Argentina.
Captain Kane said the winger is "showing that he belongs at the highest level, for Barcelona and England" and that Gordon is "relishing" being one of England's "main men".

"I think it's great," added England and Leeds striker Dominic Calvert-Lewin. "The fact that we've got top-level English players playing abroad now at top European clubs, I think it's only good for English football and us as a national team.

"You see they bring different experiences that they're learning from overseas and they bring it into this group and I think as you can see they're only growing in confidence and as players and I think it's only a positive thing."

articles.headline: Ciryl Gane survives relentless Josh Hokit to defend title in chaotic UFC 334 main event
keyFacts: Ciryl Gane defended his UFC heavyweight title against Josh Hokit via a unanimous decision at UFC 334.

body: Ciryl Gane edged a razor-thin decision to defend his heavyweight title against Josh Hokit at UFC 334.
After five rounds at the top of the Madison Square Garden card , all three judges scored the contest 48-47 in favour of Gane, the first-ever French-born UFC champion.
Hokit set an insane pace from the opening exchange and kept it going into the championship rounds Getty
Both men traded heavy leather in the one-of-a-kind heavyweight title fight Getty
Hokit dragged Gane into a dogfight from the first bell, and the champion was forced to stand and bang with the American for most of the heavyweight classic in New York.
Incredibly, the slugfest continued right through the championship rounds, as Hokit pushed a frantic pace round after round.
In fact, the main event set a new record for the most combined significant strikes ever in a UFC heavyweight fight.
Gane, however, showed his championship qualities in the later rounds, recovering from multiple scares early on to work his way back in favour on the judges’ scorecards.

Gane took an unusual path to becoming the undisputed champion. The Frenchman failed in bids for the full title against Jon Jones and Francis Ngannou early in his career, but had success in interim title bouts against Derrick Lewis and then Alex Pereira this summer. The fight was originally set for January until Harrison suffered a devastating neck injury that required immediate surgery. Now, the two look to settle their differences as rivals after sharing a gym when Harrison first broke into the sport.

articles.headline: Could universal basic income be part of the solution in an AI economy?
keyFacts: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz acknowledged that artificial intelligence's impact on work requires considering economic policies such as basic income, RND reported.
Germany's Federal Employment Agency head Andrea Nahles warned that artificial intelligence could eliminate up to 800,000 German jobs over the next 15 years.
Economist Dominik Enste said Germany will have to change social security systems and potentially tax artificial intelligence if work is replaced.
body: At the German government's 2026 "Digital Summit" in early November, Chancellor Friedrich Merz was asked by a journalist to square a difficult economic circle: If artificial intelligence could make hundreds of thousands of people redundant in the next few years, might it become necessary for the government to give people a basic income to ease the ensuing economic disaster?
Surprisingly, Merz didn't respond with a flat dismissal — as might be expected from a conservative politician known for his neoliberal, market-friendly views.

"I've always been a bit cautious about this issue in recent years," he said, as reported by the news outlet RND. "However, I'm also well aware that the issue of AI will change our working world so fundamentally that we'll have to give serious thought to many of these issues in the coming years — including the question: Is our productivity not good enough?"

What makes this ambiguity notable is that much of Merz's policies since becoming chancellor last year have involved making Germans work more: His government's planned pension reforms would see Germany's retirement age being raised. In July this year, he announced a crackdown on sick leave. And in spring last year, having barely taken office, he caused much consternation by criticizing the concept of a "work-life balance" and declaring, "We in this country must work more and more efficiently."
The impending job rupture

But those policies seem to contradict the impending realities of the labor market in an AI world. This week, the head of Germany's Federal Employment Agency, Andrea Nahles, warned that the introduction AI would cost Germany as many 800,000 jobs in the next 15 years. Though she also said AI could eventually create a similar number of jobs, clearly the socio-economic upheaval would be considerable.

Nahles is not the only leading figure concerned about job losses caused by AI. Karsten Wildberger, Germany's minister for digital transformation and government modernization, takes any opportunity he can to warn that Germany must prepare for the economic disruptions of AI.

And even for Wildberger, a former CEO of a massive retail company, part of the future economy might come down to giving people free money. He was convinced, he told the Neue Osnabrücker Zeitung in March, "that an unconditional basic income can be part of the solution to cushion the upheavals in the labor market."
Why tech bosses love UBI

Campaigners have cautiously welcomed this new openness from unexpected quarters. "It shows that in the face of technological transformation we also need to look differently at the question of how we need to secure people's economic stability," said Kirsten Herrmann, board member at the non-profit Mein Grundeinkommen (My Basic Income), which runs various projects examining the social and economic impact of UBI.

"But I also think that individual statements by politicians don't amount to a political change, of course," she told DW. "It just means that we need to enter a serious and constructive debate about what kind of a role a basic income can play."

The idea of a universal basic income (UBI) is very old: The English Renaissance philosopher Thomas More mentions it in his 1516 book Utopia, for instance. But since the 20th century, it has largely been seen as an idealistic notion adopted by leftists — that is, until some of the world's most high-profile tech bosses latched onto the idea as a way to offset the utopian advances that they said AI would bring. In 2017, Elon Musk, who had co-founded the corporation OpenAI two years earlier, predicted that a universal basic income would at some stage become inevitable.

Since then, leading figures in the AI sector, including Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, and Sam Altman, the other founder of OpenAI, have all gone on record in support of UBI (though Altman's interest has cooled somewhat since he launched a massive UBI experiment in the US in 2019).

But Herrmann says it's a "double-edged sword" when such figures mention the idea. She is not convinced that organizations like hers and people like Elon Musk want the same thing. "On the one hand, it's always nice when the debate about a basic income gets attention from prominent voices," she said. "On the other hand, the basic income that people from the tech business talk about is a kind of neoliberal basic income: They talk about what to do when there are no more profitable jobs for people, because they still actually do need people to do certain things, whereas we talk about a basic income that is meant to give people a secure economic base — before the crisis in the job market happens."
AI and basic income

What makes the comments of Merz and Wildberger all the more eyebrow-raising is that mainstream German economists have long since rejected the basic income idea. Dominik Enste, director of the democracy, society, and economic ethics department at the German Economic Institute (IW) in Cologne, dismissed the idea out of hand — AI or no AI. UBI was, he said, just too expensive, especially in a country that already has plenty of social welfare costs.

"Many economists have calculated that implementing this in many countries is financially unfeasible — in Germany, for one, simply because of the need to fund commitments that have already been made (including pension payments)," he told DW in an email.

However, he also added: "We will have to change our social security systems if work is replaced by AI and, if necessary, tax AI-generated income. But it will be a conditional basic income that still provides incentives to earn a living."

Other economists are more positive about the idea. "How this plays out depends on many choices we make, and on who makes these choices, in whose interest," said Maximilian Kasy, professor of economics at Oxford University and author of a book on the impact of AI on society. "But a lot of the current thrust is to replace workers to increase profits and increase corporate control, though this is not the only path possible."

Kasy also thinks that is a good idea, "especially if it's financed in a progressive way (so that only those at the lower end of the income distribution are net recipients)," he told DW by email. "The 'small print' matters very much, though!"

If the warnings of Wildberger, Musk, Altman et al. are to be believed, AI is already causing a bigger upheaval than any other technological advance in history: Partly because of the speed of the innovations, but also because of the scale of the potential impact: AI innovation is affecting the jobs of the traditional urban middle classes across the entire world. In 2024, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) predicted that some 40% of employment in the world would be shaped by AI innovations, and as much as 60% in rich, industrialized nations.

For her part, Herrmann thinks we are not yet asking the truly fundamental questions about the socio-economic implications of AI: Not just how do we replace the lost jobs and keep the capitalist system going, but what do we actually want to use AI for? As she puts it: "Who actually profits when we become more productive through AI? And how do we redistribute that profit to everyone?"

This, she argues, is why there needs to be more debate about how exactly AI is used in the world of work: "Which jobs are going to be replaced by AI is not some law of nature," Herrmann said. "It's something that we can shape politically and socially — and then the bigger question is: Who gets a say?"

articles.headline: US Olympic hero Kayla Harrison chokes out Amanda Nunes in fourth round to retain UFC title
keyFacts: Kayla Harrison retained her UFC women’s bantamweight title by defeating Amanda Nunes with a fourth-round rear-naked choke at Madison Square Garden.
Nunes, a former two-division champion, returned from a three-year retirement for the bout, while Harrison secured her first title defense.
Harrison stated she will make decisions about her future after struggling with the weight cut, while Nunes may return to retirement.
body: Kayla Harrison retained her UFC women’s bantamweight championship with a fourth-round submission of Amanda Nunes on Saturday night at Madison Square Garden, spoiling the comeback bid of the woman widely regarded as the greatest female fighter in MMA history.

Harrison (20-1) had plenty to prove in her first title defense against Nunes, who ended a three-year retirement for the long-awaited showdown. It was also Harrison’s first fight since June 2025, after spinal fusion surgery in January to address a neck injury forced the postponement of the bout.

Nunes (23-6) tried to wrestle with the two-time Olympic judo gold medalist and ended the first two rounds flat on her back. Harrison landed a series of short punches and elbows to the head that seemed to tire her out – she later acknowledged the difficulty of cutting weight to 135lb – as much as they damaged Nunes.

Harrison, who walked out to Eye of the Tiger while the fighter known as the Lioness stretched and bounced on her tiptoes ahead of Bruce Buffer’s introductions, wasted no time in the fourth round. Harrison grabbed Nunes by her right leg and tripped her to the canvas before taking her back and applying a rear-naked choke. Nunes quickly tapped out, to the astonishment of the packed Garden crowd.
“I think I’m still in shock,” Harrison said.
Nunes may be considered the greatest fighter in the sport’s history. Harrison staked her claim as the best right now.
Nunes walked out of the octagon on her own, while a victorious but weakened Harrison needed help returning to the locker room, championship belt firmly around her waist.
“I’ve got a lot of decisions to make when I get home,” Harrison said. “Every time I make weight, I say never again, so we’ll see.”

A UFC Hall of Famer, Nunes held championships in two weight classes, lost only once in 12 previous UFC title bouts and defeated the once-indomitable Ronda Rousey. She retired in 2023, citing burnout and a desire to spend more time with her wife as they raised their two young daughters.
She could return to retirement with her legacy as one of the sport’s greatest fighters secure.
In the main event, Ciryl Gane successfully defended his heavyweight championship, sweeping the scorecards over the five-round fight to win a unanimous decision and beat Josh Hokit.
Gane won 48-47 on all three scorecards as the pro-Hokit crowd howled in disbelief.
Gane (15-2) defeated Alex Pereira at the White House card in June and claimed the interim heavyweight title before he was promoted to undisputed champion in Tom Aspinall’s absence November.

Gane and Hokit (10-1) engaged in a slugfest that left both fighters bloodied – Hokit above the left eye, Gane from the mouth – but neither one landed any sustained offense which forced this outcome to the judges.
Hokit wore an American flag bandana and sunglasses and smirked as the decision was announced.
“I will rejoice in my suffering,” Hokit said. “I will never lose hope. I will be champion one day.”
Hokit flipped off Gane once, ducked a right, and extended a middle finger for a second time to close the third round.
The New York crowd ate it all up.
Hokit remained as crude in the cage as he is uncouth outside the octagon in hyping his fights.
Yet it was the 36-year-old Gane, who had lost to Francis Ngannou and Jon Jones in previous attempts to win the heavyweight championship, who walked out still champion.

US president Donald Trump has attended UFC events at the Garden in the past but was absent on Saturday night. Trump said last week he was offering UFC chief Dana White the job of White House press secretary, although he later said he was joking.
After bringing UFC to the White House lawn this summer, Trump brought White into the press briefing room on Monday. Trump briefly stood aside as White took questions.
White occupied his usual cageside seat and celebrated the promotion’s achievements over the decade since professional MMA was legalized in New York.

Conor McGregor won the lightweight championship in the main event of UFC’s debut card at Madison Square Garden 10 years ago. Georges St-Pierre, Daniel Cormier and Jon Jones are among the fighters who have won major championship bouts at MSG, where headlining the annual card has become a career goal for many champions.
Some fighters simply want to go out on top in New York.

Stephen Thompson had fans chanting his “Wonderboy” nickname during his retirement fight against Charles Radtke in a welterweight bout. Thompson, 43, who twice challenged for the welterweight championship, won by third-round stoppage with a spinning wheel kick to Radtke’s head. UFC played a video tribute to Thompson afterward.
“I told myself I wasn’t going to cry,” Thompson said, his voice catching. “We wouldn’t have this sport if it wasn’t for my fans.”
Thompson laid his gloves on the mat, the traditional symbolic farewell of a fighter entering retirement.

articles.headline: Francophone summit opens in Cambodia amid Rwanda-DR Congo rift
keyFacts: Leaders of the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie are meeting in Cambodia for a three-day summit amid internal disputes.
The Democratic Republic of the Congo threatened to leave the organisation if Rwanda's Louise Mushikiwabo is re-elected.
Leaders will choose the organisation's next secretary-general for a four-year term on Monday.
body: Leaders of the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie (OIF) are meeting in Cambodia amid a dispute between the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Rwanda over who should lead the association of French-speaking nations, which threatens to split the group.

The OIF is holding a three-day summit in the Cambodian capital, Phnom Penh, through Monday. A loose confederation of 90 states and governments where French is spoken or widely used, the OIF has 53 full members, five associate members and 32 observers.

French President Emmanuel Macron, who chaired the last summit in 2024 and will hand the chair to Cambodia, arrived on Saturday and met Prime Minister Hun Manet, The Associated Press news agency reported.
About 20 leaders are expected, including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Vietnamese President To Lam, Rwandan President Paul Kagame and DRC President Felix Tshisekedi.
A fight over the top job
On Monday, leaders will choose the organisation’s next secretary-general for a four-year term.
Rwanda’s Louise Mushikiwabo, who has led the OIF since 2018, is seeking a third term.

The DRC, however, which accuses Rwanda of backing the M23 armed group in the country’s east, has threatened to leave the OIF if she is re-elected. Congo, the United States and United Nations experts say Rwanda backs the M23, one of about 100 armed groups in the mineral-rich region.
Rwanda denies the allegations.

On Saturday, the DRC withdrew its candidate, Juliana Lumumba, the daughter of independence hero Patrice Lumumba, and backed Romanian former Prime Minister Dacian Ciolos to allow “consensus around a unifying candidacy”.
Rwanda’s foreign minister, Olivier Nduhungirehe, said Mushikiwabo would stay in the race. Mauritania’s Coumba Ba, a former minister, is also running, the AFP news agency reported.

Macron’s office said that most members agreed on the need for consensus and that he would take it up with his African counterparts. France is the biggest contributor to the OIF’s 2026 budget of 71.7 million euros ($79m).
Rwanda has said Macron asked Kagame to withdraw its candidate and that Kigali refused, AFP reported.

The DRC has a population of more than 110 million, roughly 40 million more than France, and is the most populous country where French is an official language. Its exit would be a blow to the organisation, which lost Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso, which announced their withdrawals in March 2025 following suspensions over military coups.
Cambodia in the spotlight
The summit’s slogan is “Reinvest in Peace for Shared Prosperity and Lasting Stability”. Activists see it as a chance to press Cambodia, a de facto one-party state, on rights.

UN Special Rapporteur Tom Andrews urged delegates to press for the release of detained activists. “No one should be detained for defending human rights, reporting on matters of public concern, or voicing critical opinions,” he said.
Macron arrived as France faces widespread protests at home. He is due to visit the Angkor World Heritage Site on Monday before leaving for Malaysia.

articles.headline: 8 Near-Perfect Sci-Fi Miniseries that Hook You in the First Episode
keyFacts: Polygon identified eight science fiction miniseries that provide complete, high-quality viewing experiences within a few days.
The list includes diverse titles such as Station Eleven, Watchmen, Bodies, Years and Years, FLCL, Scavengers Reign, Devs, and V.
These shows were selected for their ability to deliver impactful, self-contained narratives that avoid the need for multi-season commitments.
body: The best science fiction stories have a habit of going on forever. Franchises like Star Wars, Star Trek, and even Alien enter the world with such incredible momentum that we're still making sequels and spin-offs all these decades later. After all, part of what makes sci-fi so great is the opportunity to imagine alternate entire worlds, galaxies, and universes, and then explore them indefinitely. But sometimes, you just want to watch something that can be finished in a single weekend. That's where miniseries come in.

Sci-fi stories are a dime a dozen, but very few genre stories manage to make an unforgettable impact with the miniseries format. This makes sense. Shows like The Expanse or Westworld need more space to flesh out their multi-season storylines. That said, some sci-fi miniseries accomplish a lot with less. Whether you’re looking for an action-packed show or one that is more philosophical in tone, these eight entries make for a near-perfect viewing experience that can be wrapped up in just a few days.
1 Station Eleven

Stories set in a post-apocalyptic dystopia usually require some time to establish the rules of their worlds, but Station Eleven rewards us with 10 enthralling episodes that hit hard from the very start. Set 20 years after a flu pandemic that led to the collapse of human civilization, Station Eleven follows a group of survivors who make a living by performing as a theatre troupe. Instead of embracing nihilism, Station Eleven focuses on grief as a shared language between survivors, who try to heal through artistic endeavors. There’s also plenty of violent conflict, but the resolutions are satisfying and earned.
2 Watchmen

After serving as showrunner for Lost and The Leftovers, Damon Lindelof helmed Watchmen, penned as a sequel to Alan Moore and Dave Gibbons’ popular 1986 comic book. The miniseries draws from the source material, continuing the story of iconic heroes and villains like Doctor Manhattan and Ozymandias, while also introducing new characters to reflect how their world has evolved. In the show, a white supremacist group inspired by the Watchmen character Rorschach clashes with the Tulsa Police Department, who are forced to conceal their identities to avoid being targeted. Angela Abar (Regina King), also known as Sister Knight, is a detective investigating the murder of her friend, but she stumbles upon long-hidden conspiracies related to vigilantism, which has been outlawed in this reality. Watchmen excels in puzzle-box plotting, which is grounded in real-world historical trauma and a nuanced understanding of superhero mythos and how it evolves.
3 Bodies

Time travel shows like Dark have elevated the genre like never before, but Bodies reinvigorates it with just eight episodes. Based on Si Spencer and Dean Ormston’s graphic novel, Bodies opens with the appearance of a corpse in the Whitechapel area of London. The same body, however, shows up at various points in time: 1890, 1941, 2023, and 2053. The four detectives involved with the case approach it differently, as their investigation is guided by the prevailing mood of the times. This is intriguing to watch, as a detective working during World War II sports a different sensibility than someone living in the Victorian era. Bodies makes good use of its talented ensemble cast, and it's a perfect binge-watch over your next rainy weekend.
4 Years and Years

You might know Russell T Davies as the driving force behind the Doctor Who revival, but he also wrote Years and Years, a dystopian sci-fi drama that’s quite emotionally devastating. Set between 2019 and 2034, the series follows the Lyon family, who witness the rise of a controversial politician named Vivienne Rook (Emma Thompson). This is a time of great political instability in Britain. Technological progress goes hand in hand with economic upheaval, affecting the everyday lives of the Lyons. Years and Years is perfect for anyone who likes realistic sci-fi that holds up a mirror to a possible future that is more bleak than hopeful. The plausibility of the premise makes it super effective, with Rook emerging as a chilling antagonist that evokes troubling parallels to real-world politicians of the current times.
5 FLCL

The original six-episode anime FLCL is nothing short of a masterpiece. FLCL follows Naota Nandaba, a 12-year-old whose mundane suburban life is shattered by the arrival of Haruko Haruhara, an alien woman who runs him over with a Vespa and then hits him with a bass guitar. Soon, robots and weapons begin emerging from inside Naota’s head after the injury, which Haruko uses as a portal while carrying out an intergalactic mission. This coming-of-age adventure, produced by Gainax and Production I.G, sports a standout visual identity, thanks to a seamless blend of traditional cel animation and 3D CGI. FLCL works with flawed characters, creating a raw emotional resonance that feels special in this unique standalone tale.
6 Scavengers Reign

Although Scavengers Reign had the misfortune of being canceled by HBO Max after one season, this animated sci-fi show retroactively works well as a brilliant miniseries with a tantalizing cliffhanger ending. The story is about the survivors of a damaged cargo ship stranded on an alien planet, whose vivid vegetation hides unpredictable dangers. Although the survivors are separated into three groups, all of them witness an odd symbiosis between the flora and fauna of the region, along with a complexity that has never been seen before. The planet feels like a character in its own right, forcing every survivor to closely study its bizarre characteristics and life cycles. Scavengers Reign leans into a 1990s aesthetic, inducing hypnotic beauty and environmental dread at the same time.
7 Devs

Alex Garland, best known for sci-fi movies like Ex Machina and Annihilation, created Devs, a sci-fi thriller that defies straightforward analysis. A cutting-edge tech company named Amaya offers a coveted position on its mysterious quantum computing team to Sergei (Karl Glusman). When tragedy strikes, Sergei's girlfriend Lily (Sonoya Mizuno), who also works as a software engineer for the same company, becomes involved in a mystery that starts feeling more surreal and abstract by the second. Devs is Garland at his surreal, unnerving best, and the show’s eight episodes take their sweet time to arrive at a complicated conclusion about determinism and free will. Despite its slow-burn, the show keeps you hooked with its intricate structure and compelling arguments about human nature.
8 V

Any sci-fi list is incomplete without an alien invasion story, and V fits perfectly into these expectations. Well, almost. Kenneth Johnson’s (Bionic Woman, The Incredible Hulk) two-part miniseries opens with extraterrestrial beings known as the Visitors extending an olive branch as they land on Earth. They seek aid for their dying world, offering knowledge about their advanced technology in return. After the government accepts this offer, a covert infiltration begins, with Visitors rapidly gaining power in political positions. V subverts expectations by turning its invasion premise into a grounded political allegory about fascism and resistance. Instead of leaning into the tropes of the time, this 1983 show uses documentary-style realism and nuanced drama to tell a story worth remembering.

articles.headline: US judge blocks Trump’s plan to renovate historic DC golf course
keyFacts: US District Judge Ana Reyes temporarily blocked the Trump administration from closing East Potomac Park for golf course renovations.
The DC Preservation League sued, arguing that President Trump's redevelopment plan violates federal laws and makes the course unaffordable.
Judge Reyes ordered an ethics investigation into whether government lawyers repeatedly misled her about the timeline for the park closure.
body: A federal judge has ordered a temporary suspension of any work at a historic Washington public golf course, in the latest setback for US president Donald Trump’s plan to turn it into a championship-level course.

In a 30-page decision, US district judge Ana Reyes temporarily blocked the federal government from moving forward with a plan that would have closed East Potomac Park on Sunday. Trump said in an 18 October social media post that the closure would last 15 months and transform the park’s golf offerings into “one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World”.
Reyes ruled that the Trump administration’s stated reasons for closing the park were “pretextual” and that the government violated at least two federal laws “to meet an arbitrary deadline”.
“The government proposes to close a historic park, daily enjoyed by Washingtonians of all stripes, indefinitely,” Reyes wrote.
The plaintiffs argue that Trump’s plan would change the character of the accessible golf course and make it unaffordable, something the president denies.

Although Reyes ordered that the park – near the Jefferson Memorial, 2 miles (3km) south of the White House – remain open, the Trump administration does not have to maintain golf operations at the site, the judge wrote. But the government “cannot use the absence of golf operations as a reason to exclude the public,” she added.

The ruling by Reyes, who was appointed by Joe Biden and whom Trump has called a “lunatic”, is the latest instance of the federal judiciary pushing back against Trump’s sweeping efforts to redesign the nation’s capital through major construction projects.

Many of his projects, including plans for a huge ballroom at the White House, the installation of his own name on the Kennedy Center and construction of a massive arch, have been challenged in courts.
The ruling came in a lawsuit brought by the DC Preservation League, a historic preservation group that says Trump’s plan to redevelop the park violates various federal regulations and statutes.

The group’s lawyers earlier won a ruling from Reyes that blocked the National Park Service, part of the Interior Department, from cutting down trees at the park or making other irreversible modifications without advance notice.

Democracy Forward, which is representing the preservation league and two local residents in the case, said in a statement it was grateful that Reyes stopped “another one of the president’s vanity projects”.
The group’s senior legal adviser, Catherine Carroll, said: “The administration’s inexplicable drive to destroy East Potomac Park would have taken away a treasured park that could never be replaced.”
The Interior Department, Justice Department and the White House did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The lawsuit has produced several heated confrontations between Reyes and Justice Department lawyers. The judge said last month that the government’s removal of hundreds of trees from the course and failure to tell the preservation group about the work “has cost the government all of its credibility” in the case.
Reyes has ordered an ethics investigation into whether government lawyers have repeatedly misled her about the timeline for the park’s closure.
The Justice Department has accused Reyes of overstepping her authority and inappropriately belittling government lawyers. It demanded her recusal from the case, a request she denied.
Trump, who owns golf courses globally, has focused on the East Potomac Park renovations as part of his larger ambition to leave an architectural legacy across Washington.

The park has three golf courses totalling 36 holes, a miniature golf course and a paved loop popular with cyclists and runners. The proposed redesign would turn the area into a single 18-hole championship course that Trump has said could hold world-class events, such as the US Open and the Ryder Cup, while remaining open to the public.
With Reuters and Associated Press

articles.headline: GTA 6 soundtrack leak confirmed accurate with new songs from Lana Del Rey, Playboi Carti, and Keith Richards
keyFacts: A leaked tracklist for the Grand Theft Auto 6 soundtrack has been confirmed as accurate by sources at Rolling Stone and Billboard.
The soundtrack features new songs from artists including Lana Del Rey, Playboi Carti, Keith Richards, and the electronic duo Justice.
Grand Theft Auto 6 is scheduled for release on consoles on November 19.
body: Grand Theft Auto 6 is more leak than ship at this point, with the anonymous individual known as Cyberleek in particular responsible for feeding the hype machine in ways that Rockstar weren't big fans of. The latest leak came from elsewhere, however, via a video of someone handling advance copies of the vinyl soundtrack. The album's track listing is visible, and has been confirmed as accurate by Rolling Stone's sources as well as Billboard's.

articles.headline: Nationwide ground stop spills into partisan politics
keyFacts: A nationwide FAA ground stop canceled thousands of flights due to an equipment malfunction caused by old technology, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said.
Democratic lawmakers blamed the Trump administration for the disruptions, while the White House blamed the previous administration for neglecting air traffic control issues.
Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford stated that U.S. air travel is expected to return to normal by the end of Sunday.
body: The nationwide ground stop issued by the Federal Aviation Administration on Friday afternoon spilled into partisan politics throughout Saturday.

Multiple Democratic lawmakers took aim at the Trump administration after thousands of flights were canceled on Friday night and throughout Saturday. After appearing at an initial press conference alongside Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Friday night, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Saturday an equipment malfunction due to old technology was to blame for the issuance.

Gov. Kathy Hochul (D-NY) said Duffy should resign or be replaced by President Donald Trump. She also said, “Congress must launch a full investigation to determine what went wrong and ensure it never happens again.”

Gov. Mikie Sherrill (D-NJ) similarly took aim at the Trump administration, saying “the American people deserve an effective, competent federal government.” Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg also opened remarks at an event on Friday evening by ridiculing the situation.
“Instead of investing in vanity projects like the ballroom, Trump and Secretary Duffy should prioritize modernizing our air traffic control system,” Sherrill said.

The White House addressed the controversy itself on Saturday, saying that under former President Joe Biden , the FAA was focused on “inclusive language” and did “absolutely nothing to address the problems plaguing [air traffic control].” It posted a clip of then-Senator and current Vice President JD Vance asking the then FAA administrator about an “Inclusive Language Summit” that featured discussions of getting rid of the term “airman.” Trump himself has not commented on the controversy as of Saturday night.

House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) addressed calls to provide additional funding for air traffic control infrastructure in an interview earlier Saturday, saying he was working on an “aggressive legislation package” for what is a “very important investment.”
JOHNSON BACKS DUFFY DEMAND FOR ADDITIONAL FUNDING FOR AVIATION UPGRADES
Friday’s ground stop was the country’s longest in 25 years. It was finally lifted shortly after 8 p.m. on Friday night.

Travelers with plans to fly on Sunday should expect that U.S. air travel will “be back to normal by the end of Sunday,” according to Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford, who spoke with reporters in the nation’s capital on Saturday. “The worst is behind us,” he said, according to the Associated Press .

articles.headline: Judge temporarily blocks Trump from closing Washington DC golf course for renovation
keyFacts: US District Judge Ana Reyes temporarily blocked the government from closing the East Potomac Golf Links for renovations.
Reyes stated the administration violated federal laws and gave pretextual justifications to meet an arbitrary deadline.
The temporary restraining order will remain in effect until 28 November while legal proceedings continue.
body: - Published
A federal judge has temporarily blocked the US government's closure of a historic golf course and park in Washington DC.
US District Judge Ana Reyes has been overseeing a months-long challenge to the president's plans for East Potomac Golf Links, which he said would be closed from 15 November for extensive renovations.
Reyes has said Donald Trump cannot close the park or its golf course, but added that his administration was not required to actively manage either.

Trump, an avid golfer, has said his plans to upgrade the 106-year-old course will create "one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World". The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.

Declaring the current course "Trash Island", he announced in October it would be renovated over 15 months to create a space that "will be open to the Public while, at the same time, designed to the Highest Level of Golf and able to hold World Class Tournaments" - despite the ongoing litigation.

In a 30-page decision issued on Saturday, Reyes said the Trump administration's justifications for the proposed course closures were pretextual, and that the government violated at least two federal laws "to meet an arbitrary deadline."
"The Government proposes to close a historic park, daily enjoyed by Washingtonians of all stripes, indefinitely," Reyes wrote.

She said the closure "runs counter to the public interest in utilising national parkland", adding that the government had not "plausibly identified any harm it would suffer from a temporary restraining order that preserves the status quo pending further proceedings".
Her order will last until the 28 November.
The legal dispute dates back to February, when the DC Preservation League and others sued over redevelopment plans for the park.
The historic course, which sits 2 miles (3km) south of the White House, is one of three public courses run by the National Park Service in the nation's capital.
The legal fight then escalated in October, when the NPS began to cut down hundreds of trees without notifying Reyes until 15 hours before work was set to begin.
After the trees were cut, Reyes ordered the Trump administration to stop tree removal until at least 26 October and give her three business days' notice about making any other permanent changes.
Despite the work stoppage, Trump announced that the course would be closed for 15 months from 15 November to accommodate the renovations. He also shared a rendering of the course redesign.

"The current Course is old, broken, dilapidated, and of no further use or effect. It is in very poor condition, with falling, dangerous, and disease-infested trees and, importantly, a collapsing and hazardous seawall," he said in a post to Truth Social.
Reyes has since separately opened an inquiry into whether the justice department attorneys "have made misrepresentations to the court and otherwise violated ethical rules".

That included whether giving late notice to the court about the renovation plans was "done in bad faith" and whether the attorneys failed to correct previously false statements or withheld information.
She said she would carry out the inquiry with a special master, an independent third party.

articles.headline: GTA 6 Is Like The Olympics – “A Rare Cultural Moment” With Massive Ripple Effects
keyFacts: Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 launches on November 19, with experts describing the highly anticipated game as a rare cultural event.
PwC expert Bart Spiegel stated the game could shift consumer attention away from other entertainment like streaming services and movies for months.
The game's expected success may drive future investment into the broader gaming ecosystem, including advertising, payment infrastructure, and artificial intelligence technologies.
body: After years of development, multiple delays, and what can only be assumed to be one of the biggest production budgets ever, Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 launches on November 19. The game is poised to "blot out the sun," some experts believe, and its release looms so large that other gaming companies are shifting dates for their own games to stay out of the blast radius.

Francis Lawrence, the director of the new Hunger Games movie Sunrise on the Reaping, which comes out a day after GTA 6, has said he hopes people can find the time to play the game and watch his movie . In short, GTA 6 is seen by some as a black hole that will suck up time, attention, and money from the broader gaming economy--and even workplaces, as people dive into the 80-hour game they've been waiting a decade to play.

To help make sense of, and contextualize, the enormity of GTA 6's looming launch, GameSpot caught up with Bart Spiegel of the global professional services and research company PricewaterhouseCoopers, or PwC. He told GameSpot that GTA 6 is "something much bigger than a traditional entertainment launch," and is more akin to an event like the Olympics.
He believes GTA 6 is a "rare cultural moment" that "commands extraordinary attention and creates economic activity well beyond the event itself."
Jason pumping some iron in GTA 6.

Spiegel said he foresees potential shifts beyond gaming, in places like TV viewership, music consumption, social media engagement, and even travel. "In an increasingly fragmented entertainment landscape, it's rare for a single release to command this much attention across so many industries simultaneously. That's what makes this moment so significant," he said.

An economics professor recently claimed that about 1.5 million people plan to "call out sick" to play GTA 6 , and this could come at a "cost" of $1 billion to the US economy. Spiegel said people should remember that GTA 6 isn't anything new or special as it relates to taking time off work. "People regularly plan time off around major cultural and entertainment events, and this is another example of consumers prioritizing an experience they're excited about," he said.

That being said, Spiegel remarked that PwC has observed estimates suggesting time-off requests near GTA 6's release could be 9% to 17% higher than normal. "But what's more interesting to me is what happens outside the workplace. If millions of people are spending additional hours gaming, they're potentially spending less time watching television, going out to restaurants, or engaging in other activities," he said.

"And unlike a sporting event that lasts a few hours or a few weeks, this experience could keep people engaged for months. So the broader economic implications may extend well beyond a single day of missed work," he added.
"Huge net positive"

GTA 6 is expected to be an enormous success commercially--it's reportedly already sold 11 million units through pre-purchases , and that could rise to 25 million at launch . That would work out to $2 billion in revenue, which would cover the game's entire development budget and most of its marketing spend, Sensor Tower said. But many are also saying that GTA 6 represents the last of a dying breed, and that other publishers might learn all the wrong lessons from its success. Spiegel said GTA 6 is going to be a "huge net positive for the gaming industry as a whole," in part because its success will reiterate to the broader entertainment and media landscape that games are culturally significant. At the same time, Spiegel said he doesn't foresee a world in which other publishers try to replicate a blockbuster of this magnitude.

"Very few organizations have the capital, expertise, and intellectual property required to support investments on this scale. These are extraordinary events, not necessarily repeatable business models," Spiegel said.
If GTA 6 is the huge success it's projected to be, it could positively uplift the broader gaming ecosystem in a lot of ways, Spiegel continued.

"It could attract new audiences, renew investor interest, and create opportunities across advertising, payments, technology, and content creation. The real lesson isn't that everyone needs to build the next billion-dollar game. It's that gaming is an increasingly powerful part of the entertainment economy, with opportunities that extend well beyond the games themselves," he said.
Jason escaping the law in GTA 6.

Some companies, like Ubisoft, see GTA 6 not as something to be strictly afraid of. CEO Yves Guillemot says, that's because the rising tide that is GTA 6 could help drive more people to gaming overall. In fact, Ubisoft is putting out a big new update for one of its biggest games, Rainbow Six Siege, right around GTA 6's launch .
Mat Piscatella of Circana reminded people that not everyone wants to play GTA 6, and he pushed back against the theory that it's a bad business idea to launch a game near GTA 6.

"The fear of many teams to put their game in the same window as GTA is completely overblown. GTA is going to be a massive game. Of course it is. It’s going to be a huge cultural event, but not every one of the 49 million people who own a PS5 or an Xbox Series in the US is going to be interested in that," he told GamesBeat.
Could GTA 6 lead the push to more in-game ads?

Spiegel went on to say that one additional follow-on effect from GTA 6 could be something that gamers might balk at but publishers and investors might salivate over. He said that if GTA 6 succeeds in the way people expect it to, and draw people into its world for tens--or even hundreds--of hours, that could demonstrate to the wider market that it's time for gaming, as an industry, to do more with advertising.

"When millions of people are spending substantial amounts of time in interactive entertainment environments, it's natural for advertisers and investors to consider how they might participate," he said.

Advertising for mobile and social games is already commonplace, but it's less present in the PC and console gaming market. There are examples, of course, as companies have already undertaken efforts to put ads into gaming with mixed results. Gamers quickly revolted when EA put ads in a UFC game, prompting EA to pull them quickly to help quell the backlash. Despite that, EA recently announced the formation of a new EA Advertising division that will seek to put ads "directly into gameplay." That announcement didn't go over well, either, as fans pushed back against the idea of having to see ads in yet another place in their life. Other examples have been received more positively, or at least ambivalently, with a trucking company buying ad space in the American Truck Simulator series to help recruit staff .
Lucia and Jason in GTA 6.

Xbox, for its part, has big plans to put more ads in gaming. Xbox CSO Matthew Ball said advertising in console games could help with the "two-sided problem" that AAA gaming faces today. Development costs keep going up and up, and Ball said ads--as long as they're not overly in-your-face--could be a way to help developers make more money and solidify their business fundamentals. Of course, if these companies insert more ads into gaming, that doesn't mean they'll stop hawking things like DLC, microtransactions, and battle passes; they'll likely both happen in concert. As Spiegel sees it, though, if executed correctly, advertising could be a big boon for gaming.

"What's particularly interesting is that the opportunity extends beyond placing advertisements inside games. There's an entire ecosystem of digital advertising infrastructure, technology, and services that could benefit as gaming continues to grow. I expect we'll see increasing interest in those opportunities, particularly from investors looking for exposure to gaming without taking on the considerable financial risks associated with developing blockbuster titles," he said.
More investment

During the COVID years, the gaming industry saw massive revenue and player growth as people, forced to stay inside due to stay-at-home orders, turned to games to pass the time, have fun, and connect with friends. At the same time, interest rates were historically low. The cost to borrow money was so attractive that publishers ramped up significantly.

The COVID-era boost to gaming did not last, though, and the industry is now challenged, to say the least, with numerous developers cutting staff, cancelling projects, and scaling back in other ways. If GTA 6 is indeed a massive success, it could trigger renewed interest in gaming as an investment vehicle, Spiegel believes, but not necessarily exclusively for funding new games and studios. Instead, Spiegel said he foresees big investment growth for discrete elements of gaming, including advertising, payment services, and AI buildouts.

"I absolutely think a release of this magnitude will get the attention of investors, corporate executives, and private equity firms. But I don't necessarily think that translates into another wave of billion-dollar game development," he said. "The economics of producing games at this scale are incredibly challenging, and very few organizations have the resources, expertise, and intellectual property necessary to justify those investments."

"Instead, I think investors will increasingly ask how they can participate in the broader gaming ecosystem," Spiegel added. "That could mean opportunities in advertising, payment infrastructure, technology services, mobile gaming, or artificial intelligence applications that support game development."

On the subject of AI, Spiegel said he believes it's a "particularly interesting variable" because it could, at least in theory, allow developers to work more efficiently and bring down costs. There is debate about whether or not this is a genuine reality or wishful thinking on the part of AI companies trying to sell their products and services. Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick, for example, recently told Business Insider that, despite Take-Two adopting AI products for some of its workflows, the company has not seen a material decrease in its cost structure. In fact, many theorize that AI-supported workflows will only make work more intense. For his part, Spiegel said AI in game development remains only an "emerging opportunity rather than a guaranteed outcome."

"The longer-term impact may be less about creating another generation of massive blockbusters and more about directing investment toward the businesses and technologies that support the gaming economy," he said.
Who should be afraid?

A lot has already been said and written about publishers moving their release dates to avoid GTA 6, and Spiegel said he foresees dramatic possibilities for how GTA 6 could take the wind out of the sails of other entertainment near its launch. He said GTA 6 is not just a major gaming launch. Instead, he thinks it's an "event that could temporarily reshape how millions of consumers spend their time and money."

"Streaming could be particularly vulnerable. Every hour someone spends gaming is potentially an hour they're not watching a television show or movie. And because this launch falls just before the holiday season, it could make it difficult for streaming services to match the exceptionally strong viewership numbers we saw last year," he said.
The new Hunger Games movie, Sunrise on the Reaping, releases a day after GTA 6 comes out.

Movie theaters could be tested, Spiegel said, and one highly anticipated film, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, will be one to watch in particular. It comes to theaters on Friday, November 20, which is one day after GTA 6 releases. Director Francis Lawrence said he hopes fans find the time to play GTA 6 and go see his movie, but it remains to be seen what effect, if any, GTA 6's release will have on that film's performance at the box office. Spiegel said movie studios are banking on the belief that the theatrical experience "offers something consumers can't get from their living rooms."

There is a Thursday Night Football game happening on the same day that GTA 6 releases, with the Indianapolis Colts taking on the Houston Texans. Spiegel said the live-sports category overall could be "more resilient" because of its nature as an event happening live that fans of those teams, or fans of the NFL in general, feel compelled to watch live as it happens. A movie or TV show, meanwhile, is on-demand entertainment.

GTA 6 is a hugely anticipated release, and it's poised to bring lapsed gamers back into the fold, but anyone who doesn't already have a PS5 or Xbox Series X|S should prepare themselves for sticker shock. That's because, for a variety of reasons, new consoles today are actually hundreds of dollars more expensive than they were when they launched in 2020.

Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick has frankly acknowledged, "The rising cost of hardware is not a good thing." At the same time, Zelnick isn't shaking in his boots about what this means for GTA 6. He thinks GTA 6 will be so good and so compelling that people will buy in no matter what.

"I don’t think it will slow us down any because, you know, we’re delivering, we believe we’re delivering experiences that people want,” Zelnick said. “However, a lower price point for hardware would be a good thing because there’d be more hardware in people’s hands."
Who benefits?

In terms of companies, products, people, and services that could benefit from the ripple effects of GTA 6's release, Spiegel said music associated with the game could surge in listening activity. This has already happened, as streams of Tom Petty's "Love Is A Long Road" surged after the first trailer for GTA 6 used the song back in 2023. More recently, Cliff Richard's 1976 hit "Devil Woman" showed up in the GTA 6 Extended Look on Netflix, helping the song reach more people , including young people who maybe never even knew about the song. Spiegel said social media platforms could benefit from GTA 6's release as well, thanks to fans uploading gameplay clips, livestreams, and other forms of user-generated content inspired by GTA 6. Beyond this, the world of food delivery could see an uptick in activity as people opt to stay in to play GTA 6 (while in-person restaurants and other nightlife venues could take a hit).

"The broader point is that the impact could extend into parts of the economy we don't traditionally associate with gaming," Spiegel said. "For business leaders, the question is whether they're competing with this cultural moment for consumer attention or finding ways to participate in it. That's what makes this launch so much more interesting than simply tracking how many copies are sold."

articles.headline: Mamdani says he and Trump made deal over SNAP rule affecting small businesses nationwide
keyFacts: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced that he and President Donald Trump reached an agreement regarding new SNAP requirements.
President Trump agreed to grant small business owners a 90-day extension to comply with stricter produce stock rules for accepting food stamps.
Mayor Mamdani stated that the extension prevents immediate hardships and potential price increases for consumers nationwide.
body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Friday he and President Donald Trump brokered a deal on new SNAP requirements that would affect small businesses nationwide.

“I have spoken to President Trump and [Agriculture Secretary Brooke] Rollins, and as a result of those conversations, the president has agreed to give small business owners at least a 90-day extension to comply with a rule that would have affected tens of thousands of SNAP-accepting grocery stores and bodegas nationwide,” Mamadani said at a press conference . New regulations that were set to take effect last week outlined stricter requirements for the types of produce businesses could keep in stock, and stores unable to comply would lose authorization to accept food stamps.

“I want to thank the president and the secretary for their consideration of New Yorkers and the hardship that this would have imposed on millions of Americans. In doing this, President Trump has delivered relief to small business owners across our city and across America.” Mamdani said he was concerned that small businesses would be unable to comply with the regulations on time, and that consumers would face higher prices as a result.

Mamdani and Trump have developed a relatively amicable relationship despite the former’s socialist and progressive views. Mamdani has firmly maintained his anti-Immigration and Customs Enforcement stance since taking office in January, but has found common ground with Trump on other issues.

During a recent appearance on Morning Joe , the mayor was asked about working with Trump. Democrats have already begun quarreling over whether, and the extent to which, they should collaborate with Trump following their resounding victory in the 2026 midterm elections.
JUDGE OVERRIDES MAMDANI’S OBJECTIONS TO ICE SUBPOENA FOR HOMELESS SHELTER INFORMATION

“You know, I think you can. And I think what it requires is both being honest about the fact that there are significant policy disagreements the president and I have with each other, and looking for a place of shared purpose. For the two of us, it’s the welfare of New York City. And in the meetings that we’ve had, we’ve been able to free a New Yorker from ICE detention, secure a visa for a mother who would otherwise have to grieve her son from thousands of miles away, and take the steps toward building more housing in a development than this city has seen since the early 1970s. And I think that, at the end of the day, is what politics has to be: finding a way to work with whomever you can to deliver something for the people who trust.”

Centrist lawmakers who won traditionally red states such as Texas and Kansas will have to grapple with how to work alongside Democratic colleagues whose views may be offensive to voters in those regions. Intense debates regarding Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY)’s future have already begun, as many progressive Democrats view him as being representative of an establishment they’ve worked to do away with. Mamdani’s rise paved the way for the success of many socialist candidates in Democratic primaries throughout the spring and summer.

articles.headline: Fetterman admits he can’t find ‘common ground’ about Israel with far-left
keyFacts: Sen. John Fetterman stated that he no longer shares common ground with the far-left wing of his party regarding Israel.
Fetterman criticized a leadership challenge against Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer by Sen. Chris Van Hollen and called his own 2028 primary challenger pro-Hamas.
Ahmed Moor's campaign responded by stating that Moor condemns violence against civilians and that Fetterman has failed to represent Pennsylvanians.
body: Fetterman admits he can’t find ‘common ground’ about Israel with far-left
By
Madison Colombo, Fox News
Published Nov. 14, 2026, 8:28 p.m. ET
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., told Fox News on Saturday that he no longer sees “any more common ground” with the far-left wing of his party over its stance on Israel.

During an appearance on “Saturday in America,” Fetterman criticized efforts to replace Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, D-NY, with Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., and called his new 2028 Democratic primary challenger “pro-Hamas.”

“I have a strong, strong difference of opinion on Israel and the Jewish community overall now. I don’t think there’s going to be any more common ground,” Fetterman told Fox News host Kayleigh McEnany.

“Now I think if someone can’t identify [that] Iran is an enemy, and that it’s committed to destroying Israel and our nation as well, too — once again, this is the kind of individual that the Democratic Party elected,” he added.

Following midterm elections that saw Democrats regain control of both the House and Senate, Schumer is facing a challenge to his leadership. Van Hollen announced his bid to replace Schumer on Thursday, with support from progressive lawmakers, including Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich.
Fetterman said a Van Hollen victory would be troubling.

“It would be troubling if my caucus elects someone like Van Hollen, that has really made his name being very… hostile to Israel,” Fetterman said when asked if a Van Hollen win would cross a “red line.”

Fetterman said Van Hollen has made his name on strong “anti-Israel” views and also received attention after his high-profile trip to El Salvador to meet with Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran migrant deported by the Trump administration.

“Other than that, I can’t really think of what Van Hollen’s known for, but he became like a progressive darling, but I don’t see that he has a path to be leader, but overall it’s possible because just last weekend I had a lot of people protesting, demanding that we vote against Schumer,” Fetterman said.
“We have to find a way forward. After our massive wins, we immediately go back to fighting among ourselves. Can’t we just, you know, take the win?” he added.
Fetterman also called for bipartisan cooperation on the national debt, artificial intelligence, Iran and Social Security, expressing hope that Democrats could work with the White House.

“My hope [is] that our party doesn’t revert to our worst impulses. I am going to extend and just hope for bipartisan solutions and work with the White House if that’s possible. That’s where my votes will be,” Fetterman said.
Fetterman also criticized Gaza-born Palestinian-American writer and activist Ahmed Moor, who announced a 2028 Democratic primary challenge against him earlier in the week.

“This is someone that is very proud, very proud, pro-Hamas, and there are parts of my Democratic base [that] find my views more troubling or offensive, my strong support of Israel versus his views,” Fetterman said.

“I’m always going to support Israel. Iran knows that the Democratic Party, it’s very unlikely they’re [going to] hold the Iranian regime accountable. I think we deserve to have that conversation,” he added.

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Moor’s campaign pushed back on Fetterman’s remarks, saying the candidate “condemns violence against civilians by anyone” and accusing the Pennsylvania senator of failing to represent his constituents.

“Ahmed Moor is running on a platform of dignity, justice, and the rule of law. This includes ensuring that American tax dollars are spent in ways that benefit Americans, not on killing innocent people abroad. These views are in line with the majority of Pennsylvanians, who Fetterman has failed to accurately represent in Congress,” the campaign said.

The campaign added that Moor supports “an arms embargo and targeted sanctions until Palestinians have equal rights,” saying he would “fight antisemitism and anti-Palestinian racism with the same conviction.”
