articles.headline: Which NVIDIA GPU is closest to the PS5? The answer isn't so simple
keyFacts: Digital Foundry reported that the NVIDIA RTX 2070 Super graphics card best matches the base PS5 APU performance.
The 16GB RTX 5060 TI and AMD Radeon RX 9060 XT offer comparable performance to the PS5 Pro horsepower.
Comparing PC graphics cards to console hardware is complicated because consoles use unified APUs and closed-source systems.
body: Which NVIDIA GPU is closest to the PS5? The answer isn't so simple
It's a bit like comparing apples and oranges, but this NVIDIA GPU will give you the closest results to a PS5

There's no getting around it: We're in an era where it's never been more financially-punishing to buy either a new console or PC hardware. Given that we're now dealing with a tech-savvy Sophie's Choice between a PS5 and the most affordable gaming PC you can put together for similar money, value has to be taken into consideration. Is mid-range PC gaming really that much better than what the current consoles can provide?

In an age where Sony and AMD are teasing the GPU tech they're building for the next PlayStation, it's understandable folks want to compare and contrast modern console and PC tech. If you're lucky enough to own a PS5 Pro before GTA VI launches, I say stick with the kit you have. Of course, there are also exceptions where high-end gamers might want to invest in PC hardware, so let's get into when those particular, pixel-counting scenarios make sense.
What GPU offers the same power as the PS5?

First of all, this is a bit of an awkward question, but we'll get to that. Are you happy with your PS5? Then keep being happy with your PS5. As someone who has been building PCs since 2004 — yes, I'm ancient — I can't recommend assembling a custom gaming rig in an era where RAMaggeddon has hideously skewed the prices of computer components. But if you really want to know what GPU most closely aligns to the PS5's graphics solution, I can point you in the right direction ... with caveats.

According to the frame-counting wizards at Digital Foundry, the graphics card that best matches the base PS5's APU is the NVIDIA RTX 2070 Super. Notice that I said "APU" rather than "GPU". That's because the PS5, like the Xbox Series X, uses a central chipset that handles both GPU and CPU tasks in a single processor.

As for the 2070 Super, this card is now three generations old, so it's hardly cutting edge by modern standards. Thanks to our current AI-obsessed timeline though, the cheapest model of this now seven-year-old card currently costs $280 on Amazon. That's around 53 percent of the $600 PS5 Digital Edition.

If you're wondering how to buy a GPU in 2026, you really should be looking at the second-hand market. The cost of new cards right now is utterly unhinged, so I'd never recommend dropping the thick end of $300 on a GPU that launched in 2019. Specs-wise, the 2070 Super has 8GB of GDDR6 memory, but that's not an apples to apples comparison with the PS5's system-wide 16GB of GDDR6 unified memory. The 2070 Super can produce PS5-level performance under the right conditions, but comparing the PS5's APU to Team Green's aging GPU isn't a straightforward prospect.
Is the RTX 5060 stronger than the PS5 Pro?

In September 2026, the fifth gen NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 was the second-most used card according to the Steam Hardware & Software Survey with 4.40 percent market share. This lower end Blackwell GPU supports the controversial DLSS 5 that has made the internet so upset. It also boasts 8GB of GDDR7 memory with a base clock of around 2280 MHz. Currently, you'll struggle to find this card retailing for less than $500.

Enter the PS5 Pro. Sony's supercharged system now costs an inflated $1,250 (it originally launched in late 2024 at $700). In the middle of a PS5 Pro shortage, GTA 6 is only making things worse. Talking specs, the big boy PS5 leans on a custom AMD Zen 2 8 core/16 thread "Trinity" APU. While this represents a major boost over the standard PS5 in terms of GPU performance, in reality the CPU bump is only around 10 percent. That's why, in spite of the best efforts of PSSR, many Pro titles continue to fall below the sort of mid-range PC performance results you'd hope from a $1,000 box.

From a horsepower perspective, the 16GB RTX 5060 TI model and AMD's Radeon RX 9060 XT provide the best comparable performance to the raw horsepower of the PS5 Pro. But again, it's not a like-for-like comparison. With the right settings tweaks and a capable gaming CPU, either of these cards can outgun Sony's prosumer console. Yet the simplicity of Sony's $900 machine undoubtedly makes it incredibly user-friendly, and thus appealing for folks who just want to experience GTA VI in the best fashion possible.
Why comparing a graphics card to a console GPU is complicated

There are a bunch of reasons why it's unfair to compare open-ended PC setups to closed-source console hardware. Talking about the base PS5, we're dealing with a custom AMD RDNA 2 GPU that acts alongside a CPU on a single chip. There's no directly comparable piece of hardware in the PC space. Developers have routinely hit 60 FPS/supersampling, near-4K results on PS5 and PS5 Pro through canny development.

Sure, the RTX 2070 Super can generally match PS5 performance in certain games, but that's only through the lens of what that particular GPU is capable of. It doesn't take into account the broader, component-wide setup of a modern gaming PC you'd need to assemble in order to match the performance of the most powerful console ever built.

The CPU and the amount and type of RAM you pair with a card that's roughly on the level of PS5's APU matters massively. Scrimp on the processor front and you'll quickly be CPU-bound, meaning even an RTX 5090 couldn't save your console-shaming bacon. Building or buying a gaming PC needs a lot of consideration, especially during our currently ruinous financial times. If you want 4K gaming without hassle for less than $1,000, a PS5 is absolutely the way to go. Wondering how long you can expect a PS5 to last? It should be years, so there's no reason to sweat over the longevity of Sony's massively successful console.

Both the standard PS5 and the amped up PS5 Pro are outstanding consoles. Using AMD APU solutions, they hit pleasing, 4K results with smooth frame rates. Mid-range graphics cards when paired with decent gaming CPUs are going to cost a lot more. For 60 FPS/4K results with reasonable ray tracing, a PS5 or PS5 Pro will do you just fine. That said, if you want cutting edge path tracing at 120 FPS, a gaming rig with a high-end GPU is where it's at.

articles.headline: SpaceX returned its Starship rocket on Saturday—but there's a catch
keyFacts: SpaceX successfully captured its Starship upper stage using mechanical arms on the launch tower in Texas on Saturday.
The technical achievement marks a significant step for SpaceX toward developing a rapidly reusable rocket.
The rocket returned from orbit and transitioned to a vertical position before being snagged by the tower.
body: STARBASE, Texas—The black and silver ship fell out of the sky, emerging from the cloud deck near the very end of its flight. Incongruously, the rocket flew horizontal until the last moment when three Raptor rocket engines ignited and it swooped into a vertical position.

Slowly, gently, haltingly, the Starship upper stage eased its way toward the waiting tower where two arms extended outward, awaiting expectantly. The margins are so incredibly narrow. Two nubs on either side of the rocket, each protruding only about one foot, were the only purchase the rocket would have on the arms.

Then, less than a minute after it came into view, the Starship upper stage was snagged by the launch tower, as snug as you like. And so it was all over. SpaceX, nearly a quarter of a century after its founding, had just taken a hugely significant step toward developing and optimizing a massive, rapidly reusable rocket.
We are dazzled

This was a breathtaking feat; a brilliant technical achievement that required the best engineering minds to think through a million different, difficult problems. And on Saturday evening, following a handful of practice runs into the Indian Ocean, they did it before the entire world.

Watching Starship launch from here a little less than a day earlier, and knowing it had orbited the planet multiple times, added to the sense of unreality in seeing this spaceship return to Earth under its own power, and be captured by the tower.

It felt like stepping into the future. SpaceX has dazzled us before, by landing rockets on barges and returning humans to space with Crew Dragon. But this flight took things to another level. Starships are huge. They carry a huge amount of energy coming back from orbit. And until a few years ago, it seemed beyond fantastical to think about capturing a rocket with what are essentially outsized chopsticks.
Nevertheless, it happened.
Rapid reuse is firmly on the horizon

Humans have built reusable spacecraft that flew into orbit before. In the 1970s, flush with confidence after the triumphant Moon landings, NASA designed and built several Space Shuttles. They had solid rocket boosters that were fished from the ocean and reused. The large orange external tank was not recovered after each flight, but the orbiters went to space for two weeks, or even longer, before returning to Earth and landing on a runway.

articles.headline: Where was Nvidia’s security team?
keyFacts: Nvidia chief security officer David Reber stepped down in August for health reasons, followed months later by CEO Jensen Huang amid questions about his relationships.
Reports showed Huang had affairs with Nvidia employees and an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore firm suspected by U.S. investigators of funneling Nvidia chips to China.
Experts stated that corporate security teams often face limited resources and narrow mandates, making it difficult to detect insider threats and foreign intelligence operations.
body: Outsiders had little reason to notice when Nvidia’s longtime chief security officer and head of product security stepped down in August. Just two and a half months later, CEO Jensen Huang himself left the company over growing questions about his extramarital relationships — starting with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore data center company that U.S. investigators suspect of funneling Nvidia chips to China, then widening to reports about two separate affairs with Nvidia employees.

At the time, David Reber, who spent four years as CSO and seven at Nvidia overall, said he was leaving for health reasons. “This wasn’t a pivot I had planned. But I know what needs to come first: family and health,” he wrote on LinkedIn in late August, disclosing that he’d been diagnosed with young-onset Parkinson’s more than two years ago.

Reber’s replacement, Saša Zdjelar, previously spent 17 years at ExxonMobil in Houston, leaving as a senior IT manager before spending one year at Salesforce and several years at the cybersecurity company ReversingLabs. Zdjelar didn’t respond to questions Thursday about the transition or what the security team knew.

Nothing public connects Reber’s or Zdjelar’s role changes to the Megaspeed matter, but it seems fair to wonder what Nvidia’s security team knew about the government’s scrutiny of Megaspeed and about Huang’s relationships, and whether anyone raised concerns. Reber didn’t respond to questions Thursday. Nvidia also has not answered our related questions.

Relationships between a CEO and his employees typically fall to HR, legal and the board, not security. But security specialists say any affair — even one inside the office — can give a foreign intelligence service leverage over an exec who wants it kept quiet. And Huang’s relationship with an executive at Megaspeed, a company under federal investigation, wasn’t an office matter at all. (Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing.)

Still, spotting the clues isn’t easy. The way intelligence services collect information, much of it through everyday conversation rather than hacking, makes it especially difficult for security teams to identify risks, according to retired senior intelligence officer Nicholas Eftimiades, who says he has trained more than 1,000 corporate security professionals.

Some people inside Nvidia clearly knew parts of the picture. Nvidia’s top lawyer was engaged with the government’s Megaspeed inquiry more than a year ago, The New York Times reported earlier this week. (Nvidia has said it regularly contacts officials.) Reports about Huang’s relationships with employees suggest colleagues also knew of them, even if the behavior is not expressly forbidden by Nvidia’s code of conduct. The Times cited five Nvidia employees who said he was involved with a vice president who reported directly to him, and Reuters, citing two people, later reported a second relationship. What’s unclear is whether any of that reached security.

Even if it had reached Nvidia’s security team, Eftimiades, who wrote Chinese Espionage Operations and Tactics in 2020, said a security team’s resources are often limited. For one thing, they’re often underfunded because, unlike some other cost centers, they don’t drive revenue. It’s astonishingly common for CEOs to answer a security team’s warnings with “not a nickel more than compliance,” he said.

Many companies also define security overly narrowly, specialists say. In an opinion piece in The Hill, Don Aviv, CEO of the corporate investigations firm Interfor International, and author Jeremy Hurewitz, wrote, “Too many companies still approach security primarily as a matter of protecting facilities, preventing cyberattacks, and responding to physical threats.” The two argued that “[s]ecurity teams need to pay greater attention to insider threats, including the cultivation of executives and employees by foreign intelligence services, suspicious business relationships, conflicts of interest and attempts to obtain sensitive information through trusted personal contacts.”
It would be surprising if Nvidia’s security team didn’t have a more expansive remit than most companies given its scale and business partners, but it’s possible.

In fairness, some of it is simply beyond what any team can do. Speaking generally, not about Huang, Eftimiades offered a hypothetical in which a CEO complains that he can’t do something because “I’m fighting a board who doesn’t want to do this.” That tells an intelligence asset who the obstacle is. The service then asks, “Who’s the sticking point here?” and looks for ways into that person’s email and phone.

What a rival intelligence service wants is often less technology than policy insight, including who’s pushing to change export rules and who the biggest blocker is. “Intel world tends to be like cancer,” he said. “Once it gets into the body, it looks to spread and looks to reach out.”

The playbook isn’t new, Eftimiades added, “particularly for China.” Any executive dealing with the country “will tell you that they’ve been approached.” He said there are also “tons of diplomat stories” of U.S. diplomats walking into a hotel room to find a woman on the bed. He said what’s newer compared with Soviet era spying is the relationships these services cultivate now often last years, not weeks.

Technology can augment that human intelligence, Eftimiades said, pointing to IMSI catchers as one example. The devices mimic a cell tower so that nearby phones connect to them. A basic version can cost about $1,000 and fit in a suitcase, he said, though government-grade models cost far more, and there were a couple of cases involving Chinese espionage where these factored in last year.

Eftimiades says no one knows yet if the devices were used against Huang, whose phone was presumably hardened such that compromises could be detected, if not stopped altogether. But what Nvidia’s security team knew, and whether it could have acted on it, will only become clearer as the board’s independent investigation and federal inquiries proceed.

In the meantime, Eftimiades said he hopes the whole episode is “a wake-up call” for U.S. industry, which he said is mostly “clueless” about China’s tactics. “We have lost trillions [of dollars] in intellectual property,” is his guess. “Whatever we think we’re doing isn’t working.”

articles.headline: Some GTA 6 Box Copies Reported To Have Download Code Issues With No Disc To Fall Back On
keyFacts: Players report that physical copies of Grand Theft Auto VI contain no game discs and are missing or invalid download codes.
Social media users claim some boxes arrived without codes or with codes that were already redeemed by others.
Rockstar Games has not yet responded to requests for comment regarding the reported issues with the game's retail packaging.
body: After a decade and change, Grand Theft Auto VI finally drops this week. Not just one of the most overwhelmingly anticipated games in years, but a hard stress test for a future without physical media. Around the same time that Sony revealed their plans to sundown hard copies, Rockstar confirmed that their upcoming blockbuster will ship without discs. With days left, players who picked up advance retail copies are reporting issues with the download code inside. These range from the codes being claimed in advance or missing entirely.
“Can you imagine the excitement of receiving GTA VI, after having pre-ordered it weeks ago, only for it to arrive without the code?” posted McKuin, who seems to be having this exact problem.
Puedes imaginar la ilusión de recibir el GTA VI después de reservarlo hace semanas y que te llegue sin el código.
(No es un código que se raspa literalmente viene impreso así)@SoyAlexWhite #rockstargames #playstation #GTA6 #gtaiv pic.twitter.com/eXfEsGkB1a
— McKuin (@MrMckuin) November 13, 2026

Last week, excited Grand Theft Auto players could pick up “physical copies” ahead of launch. While the boxes contain no disc, they do contain a code that would enable the console to preload the game for that magical day. Over the last 24 hours, grievances about the codes have spread across social media, assuming there’s even a code to speak of.

Within the lining of the game’s cover sheet is a grey, patterned line where the code is meant to be. While it resembles a scratch-off strip, the code is simply printed on top. As certain players report their codes to be claimed in advance, some theorize it’s possible to shine a hard light at the side of the box, potentially revealing the code without it ever leaving the store. That said, our own editor-in-chief attempted to recreate this trick on his copy to no avail. Other members of the press are experiencing the same. Some believe that international copies, especially those in PAL regions, may have been packaged differently. But this is a speculation layered on top of another speculation. Like all hearsay about Grand Theft Auto it demands a chunky grain of salt.

More believable, and arguably more devastating, are players who are claiming their copy arrived without any code at all. This is a woe that we’ve seen before, requiring little more than a printer having an off-moment. Eons ago a couple copies of Batman: Arkham City arrived without their dedicated DLC codes, but that only locked out the Catwoman prologue. Now those who have paid full price, in advance, get nothing. A gut punch and an omen of how small mishaps can devastate harder in a world without physical media.

Numerous images and videos of people with code-less boxes have emerged on platforms like Reddit and X, with others claiming they’ve been refused refunds or stonewalled by Rockstar’s support line. That said, the rumor milling around Grand Theft Auto is a cottage industry in and of itself. Always flex your skepticism on this subject matter. The ‘light trick’ explanation feels like a bit of a yarn, but potential misprints are well within the realm of possibility.
We have reached out to Rockstar for comment.

articles.headline: Trump Posts More Than 40 Images Of Latest Renovation Obsession Amid Heated Legal Battle
keyFacts: Donald Trump posted dozens of photos showing damage at Washington's East Potomac Park while advocating to redevelop its golf course.
Preservation groups filed an emergency request to block the closure, prompting a judge to express skepticism over administration motives.
The park is slated to close Sunday, pending a ruling from the judge.
body: President Donald Trump posted dozens of images on Saturday of Washington, D.C.’s East Potomac Park and Golf Links, an area he has dubbed “Trash Island,” amid a legal battle to close the park and redevelop the golf course.

“Trash Island is currently the Worst Golf Course anywhere in the World, but the Department of the Interior is going to make it into the Best Golf Course anywhere in the World,” Trump wrote on Truth Social in a post topping 300 words.
The images Trump posted showed flooding, damaged fences and various debris. In all, the president shared 44 photos, though some were the same photos posted twice.

On Friday, U.S. District Judge Ana C. Reyes expressed skepticism over the administration’s motives for its plans to close the park and golf course, after preservation groups filed an emergency request to block the closure. The park is slated to close Sunday, pending a ruling from Reyes, who Trump previously called a “crazed lunatic” and suggested “may be insane?”

The administration has argued the closure needs to happen due to safety concerns, and because the trust that operates the golf course will not be operating it anymore. The trust’s lease for the golf course was terminated by Trump’s Department of the Interior.
Federal officials have insisted that they are not closing the park because of designs on overhauling the golf course and turning it into, as he has put it, a “world class” facility.
Last month, Reyes temporarily blocked the administration from cutting down more trees at the site after it felled hundreds — something officials also said was unrelated to Trump’s renovation plans.

Nevertheless, Trump in his Saturday post accused Reyes of not wanting his administration to “quickly and inexpensively fix up” the golf course. He added that he believed she would ultimately come around and rule in his favor.
“Trash Island, after years of laughter and scorn, will evolve into something very special, something which the Judge will be able to take great pride in seeing!” he wrote.

articles.headline: Forage and fight for ingredients in a magical 1960s Italy and whip up some tasty meals Cooking Mama style in The Snackbar at the End of the World
keyFacts: The Snackbar at the End of the World is a newly announced action-adventure game set in a magical, post-apocalyptic 1960s Italy.
Players forage for ingredients, fight mutated crops, and prepare Italian dishes using minigames similar to Cooking Mama.
The developers stated the game contains no AI-generated content and currently has no official release date.
body: If a game is about cooking, at minimum I'll have to give it a quick testspin. Outside of this whole writing about video games thing, my other lot in life is soul bound to food, so I'm always curious to see how the two can be mixed together. And earlier this week, The Snackbar at the End of the World was revealed, a wonderfully cartoonish action-adventure game set in a magical, slightly post-apocalyptic version of 1960s Italy where you go out and forage for ingredients while fending off monstrous crops before turning them into tasty meals back in your struggling restaurant.

First up, I just have to gush over the artstyle a bit. The whole game is hand-drawn with a colourful, comic book look that has an impressive sense of depth to it. It gives off a deep love of Italian architecture and landscapes, and that admiration clearly extends to the food too. Once you've gotten the ingredients you need, you then, loosely in the vein of Cooking Mama, prepare them and make various classic Italian dishes by performing some quick minigames. Simple, but charming! The rest of the time you're off killing some ghoulies that look like mutated fruit and veggies, with the occasional fungus-possessed hog and, uh, haunted statues? I think?

I'm also quite pleased about two points made on the game's Steam page. First is the content description: "This game features cartoon violence, sensitive political themes set in a fictional world, and depictions of an oppressive government committing crimes against its citizens." There is clearly a romantic quality to the game and I'd be worried if it didn't acknowledge any of the political context of the decades preceding.

The other line reads, "Every sound effect, musical note, design decision, and line of code is human-made. Because this game is about human relationships and delicious food – and that’s not a story we would ever trust AI to tell." Thank the lord! Right now there's no release date attached to The Snackbar at the End of the World, unsurprising given it was only announced this week. But while we all wait for a date, you could perhaps join me in throwing it a wishlist on Steam.

articles.headline: Watch SpaceX successfully execute the first ‘chopstick’ catch of Starship
keyFacts: SpaceX successfully captured the Starship vehicle with its Mechazilla launch and catch tower for the first time.
CEO Elon Musk said success is likely on future flights despite an abort that caused the booster to detonate over the Gulf of Mexico.
SpaceX is currently trying to determine the cause of the booster landing abort.
body: After aborting a planned catch of Starship Flight 15’s booster, SpaceX successfully captured Starship with its “Mechazilla” launch and catch tower for the first time. The company has performed ‘chopstick’ catches of its boosters before, but this is the first time the maneuver has successfully been executed on the Starship vehicle itself.
Watch SpaceX successfully execute the first ‘chopstick’ catch of Starship
SpaceX captured Starship using the arms of ‘Mechazilla’ its launch and catch tower for the first time.

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said during the company’s third-quarter earnings call that “success is not guaranteed on these first flights, but I’d say it’s more likely than not that this succeeds next flight.” While not a complete success, in that the company was unable to recover the entire launch vehicle, it still stands as a milestone for the Starship program. And, since it has previously caught boosters on previous launches, there is reason to believe the failure today was not an insurmountable obstacle. SpaceX is still trying to determine what caused the booster to abort its landing and detonate over the Gulf of Mexico.
In the video above, you can watch Starship plunge through the clouds, flip vertically, and, with surprising grace, ease itself between the waiting arms of Mechazilla at around 4:20 PM ET.

articles.headline: Justice Alito warns America must preserve 3 core principles regardless of country’s ‘atmosphere’
keyFacts: Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito stated that Americans must preserve freedom of speech, religious liberty, and racial equality to maintain the republic.
Alito delivered his remarks during a fireside chat at the National Lawyer's Convention in Washington D.C.
Alito confirmed that the 2026 midterm results did not change his plans to remain on the Supreme Court.
body: Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito recently laid out three principles Americans must cling to to ensure the integrity of the republic: freedom of speech, religious liberty and racial equality.

"I'm not saying we're entering the dark age, but these are things that we have to preserve no matter what the atmosphere is in the country or the world at the time," Alito said during a fireside chat with Mollie Hemingway, editor-in-chief at the Federalist, which followed the Antonin Scalia Memorial Dinner at the 2026 National Lawyer's Convention in Washington D.C.

The remarks come on the heels of the blue tsunami of the 2026 midterms, with Republicans losing 42 House seats and eight Senate seats, with the Alaska U.S. Senate race still uncalled. Democrats are set to take control of Congress with eight lawmakers backed by the Democratic Socialists of America. Both incoming and returning members have pressed for investigations and subpoenas targeting President Donald Trump and his administration.
DEMOCRATS SEIZE HOUSE CONTROL IN STUNNING BLUE TSUNAMI, VOW RETRIBUTION AGAINST TRUMP ADMIN
Alito's remarks also come amid the ongoing Iran war, which has destabilized oil supply chains across the globe, causing the price of goods and gas to jump.
The 76-year-old jurist said preserving freedom of speech is paramount, warning that "you cannot have Democratic self-fulfillment if you cannot have robust free speech."
"Even speech that is hurtful to some of the people who hear what is being said," Alito said.

He also stressed the importance of freedom of religion, even as the Supreme Court is set to rule on at least two major cases this term centered on religious freedom : St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy and Grand v. City of University Heights.
SUPREME COURT OFFERS SUPPORT FOR CATHOLIC PRESCHOOLS CHALLENGING STATE FUNDING REQUIREMENTS
"I think that we have placed religious liberty on a sounder footing than it was on 20, 25 years ago," Alito said.

"Religious liberty is central to human dignity, and in a society that is as religiously diverse as this country, we've got people who adhere to practically every religion that exists in the world," Alito continued. "We are not going to be able to get along, I think, amicably, productively, if we don't respect everybody's right to follow whatever religion they want, or for people of faith, they're also free to do that."
"That's essential," Alito said.
He rounded off his trifecta by saying that America must maintain racial equality, declaring it "essential for our pluralistic society."
FEDERAL JUDGE TOSSES TRUMP ADMIN HARVARD ADMISSIONS LAWSUIT, LEAVES DOOR OPEN TO FUTURE CHALLENGE

"That is the principle that Dr. Martin Luther King famously articulated in his speech at the Lincoln Memorial, where he said he looked forward to the day when children would be judged by the content of their character and not by the color of their skin," Alito said.
"If we don't hold to that principle, then I think the society is going to start to come apart," Alito said.

The Supreme Court agreed in October to hear Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education this term, a challenge brought by parents of Asian American students alleging that a Maryland school district’s admissions policies unlawfully discriminate despite appearing race-neutral.

Alito mentioned the Supreme Court's 2023 ruling in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard , which ended affirmative action in college admissions , as among the most consequential rulings from the Supreme Court in the past few decades.
TRUMP CHEERS ALITO STAYING FOR ANOTHER SUPREME COURT TERM: 'ONE OF THE GREATEST OF ALL TIME'

Alito's discussion comes as questions swirl about his possible plans to retire. In a Bloomberg article published after the midterms, Alito said that the Democrats' sweep did not change his plans to stay on the Supreme Court.
Alito, nominated by President George W. Bush, has served on the bench since 2006.
"With those, with those 20 years, I jumped to 42nd in the the list of all-time service by Supreme Court justices," Alito said.

articles.headline: Italy fines Meta €805m over accessing users' photos
keyFacts: Italian regulators fined Meta €805m for accessing Android users' photos without their specific consent.
Italy's Data Protection Authority said Meta failed to properly inform about 20 million users about the gallery access feature.
The regulator gave Meta 60 days to disable the feature by default and seek users' consent separately.
body: - Published
Italian regulators have fined social media giant Meta â¬805m (Â£670; $887m) for accessing Android users' photos without their specific consent.
Italy's Data Protection Authority said Meta did not properly inform about 20 million smartphone users that it had access to their photos and videos via a feature of the Facebook app.
It has given Meta 60 days to disable the feature by default and seek users' consent separately.
The fine is among the largest an Italian authority has ever imposed on a tech giant.
The charge is related to a feature which suggests photos and videos from a user's phone gallery as ideas for posts.

Facebook requested access to users' photo galleries through a single app-wide authorisation. According to the Italian regulator, a preceding notice did not make clear that this would also allow Facebook to generate suggestions based on photos in their gallery.

The regulator said it took into account "the high number of people affected" and the fact it is "still ongoing for those who have not updated the app and for those who have already given their consent to the system".
It also cited "Meta's lack of co-operation".
The BBC has reached out to Meta for comment.
Last month, Meta, which is also behind Instagram and WhatsApp, was hit with its largest fine ever for its business practices.
A US judge in New Mexico ordered the company to pay $25bn (Â£18.6bn) after it found that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data.

articles.headline: Fuel crisis and protests pressure Chile's far-right president
keyFacts: Chilean President José Antonio Kast faces a 24% approval rating due to rising fuel costs, controversial prisoner sentence reductions, and widespread public protests.
Truckers recently blockaded major highways over fuel prices, prompting the government to submit a bill to Congress to reverse planned fuel price increases.
Protests are expected to grow in Santiago if the government fails to address the rising cost of living while pursuing budget cuts.
body: Fuel crisis and protests pressure Chile's far-right president
SANTIAGO, Chile — Chile's ultraconservative president finds himself on the back foot after just eight months in power.

José Antonio Kast, a politician who spent a career railing against progressive issues, reproductive rights and welfare policies from the extreme fringes of right-wing politics, now finds himself with just 24% approval in the polls.

It is less than a year since Kast stormed to the presidency in December 2025 by avoiding all mention of his hardline stances on social matters, focusing instead on two hot-button issues whipped up in the national media: illegal immigration and public security.
But rather than pressing ahead with those at the top of his agenda, he has floundered. And as elsewhere around the Americas and worldwide, rising costs of living have come to hit him hard.
"Our salaries are maybe 20% of a European income, but with a similar cost of living – it's terrible," said Simón Echavarría, a 30-year-old architect, at a march in Santiago on Friday evening.

"We want to protest against the measures that have set us back on environmental issues, on human rights, even reducing the sentences of pedophiles – they are implementing things that nobody asked for," he said.
Behind him, heavily armed police blocked the streets and fired water cannons at protesters chanting and waving flags in the square.

Much of the recent ire stems from the revelation last month that Kast's government had signed decrees to cut the sentences of 56 prisoners whose crimes range from the rape of children to dictatorship-era human rights violations.
Kast has since admitted that this was an "error", but came out in support of the undersecretary who signed the decrees nonetheless.
But beneath the more egregious moves Kast has made in his first year in power is simmering discontent over affordability.
In July, Kast's government chose not to apply an anti-inflation tool available to the Chilean state to ease the rise in fuel prices brought about by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.
Protests exploded as prices shot up overnight and motorists joined long queues at gas stations to fill their tanks before the rise came into effect.
This week, Chile's formidable truckers' unions blockaded two major highways in an effort to exert pressure on the government and address high fuel prices.
On Friday, the strike was broken after the government backed down, sending a bill to Chile's congress which will reverse planned fuel price rises.
It is expected to be approved this month, but public anger continues to grow over the cost of living.

Politicians across the Americas who have enthusiastically aligned themselves with President Donald Trump are facing challenges similar to those confronting the U.S. administration, as rising fuel prices and the cost of everyday goods fuel public discontent.

In Argentina, far-right libertarian Javier Milei faces reelection in less than a year, with 60% of the country disapproving of his leadership amid spiraling inflation. In Peru, President Keiko Fujimori is also facing growing discontent, with 53% disapproving of her government, according to a recent Ipsos poll.
At the march in Santiago on Friday, 30-year-old veterinarian Patricia Pereira said that she was concerned about cuts to science funding, but that her discontent ran deeper.
"Here in Chile, it was a hard-won victory for children to have free education, achieved through protests, and now even that's also being called into question," she said.
Protests are likely to grow in Santiago if the government fails to address the rising cost of living. President Kast has shown little sign of doing so.
To the contrary, his budget proposal is making its way through Congress, with the government seeking cuts to education, culture, science and a host of social programs.

articles.headline: I Let My Apple Watch Eavesdrop on My Conversations for 2 Weeks
keyFacts: Apple Watch models introduced Audio Intelligence, an optional feature featuring Siri Recap and Live Rewind to record and summarize daily conversations.
The CNET reviewer found Siri Recap useful for structured work meetings, but inaccurate and prone to mixing up unrelated daily conversations.
Apple stated the features will be released publicly later this year.
body: We’ve long suspected that our devices are listening to us, but what about when we invite them to do it? That’s what testing Audio Intelligence has felt like on the Apple Watch. But despite how disturbing it may sound to have your smartwatch listening and taking notes of your entire day, the reality has been a lot more mundane.

Along with the general sensor, processor, and battery upgrades, the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 introduced Audio Intelligence, a new set of features that allows the watch to listen in on conversations.
Siri Recap generates summaries of what you’ve discussed throughout the day, while Live Rewind gives you a transcript of the last 15 seconds of audio in case you missed something.
It’s similar functionality as AI-powered recording pins like Plaud or Amazon’s Bee, but within the context of your smartwatch and without the additional cost or subscription.

And it’s completely optional. You have to first opt-in to the features to activate them, then choose to turn the feature you want on whenever you want to start using it. Then you can leave it on all day, set it on a schedule or toggle it manually whenever you need it. If you’re like me and forget that it’s on, you get reminders that it’s still listening or to check your recaps.
The fact that you have so much control over whether you use it and how much helped ease the creepy factor for me, but there’s still everyone else to consider.

Beyond a barely audible chime when I double-click the Digital Crown to activate Live Rewind, there’s no way to alert others that the feature is in use and that whoever’s in earshot is inadvertently getting roped into my little experiment as well. Other wearables like smart glasses have an indicator light on the front to alert spectators when they’re recording video.

Apple has built-in privacy safeguards for the audio, how it’s processed and then deleted. I’ve broken all that down in a separate Audio Intelligence FAQ. This is about what it’s like to use it in the wild.

I’ve been testing Audio Intelligence in the WatchOS 27.3 (and iOS) public beta for two weeks. Because this isn’t the final version (Apple says it will release publicly later this year), consider this a sneak preview.
Live Rewind: Late to the trigger
Let’s get Live Rewind out of the way because there’s not a lot to say about it. Whether from a lack of muscle memory (or usefulness), I’ve had to go out of my way to remember the feature exists.

I figured it’d come in handy for those “come again?” moments during conversations, but the reality is that it’s just easier to ask someone to repeat what they said than remember to double-press the Digital Crown at just the right moment. I can see it being more useful when you’re listening to a presentation or other event.

Fifteen seconds go by a lot faster than I expect and by the time I realize something might be worth revisiting, the person has moved on with the conversation. I either missed what I intended to get or just captured the silence after.
Siri Recap: Good at meetings, bad at life

Siri Recap has been more useful, though it’s still hit-or-miss. The feature gives you high-level summaries of what it heard — it doesn’t provide a transcript to review, and it doesn’t identify who said what. It shines brightest during dedicated meetings when there’s a single conversation to follow rather than a jumble of unrelated discussions.
One success story: I was moderating the chat for our iPhone Duo live folding test on YouTube while Matthew Murray, CNET’s lab director, answered viewer questions on the stream.

I thought I’d caught the gist of what he was saying, but the typing must’ve distracted me more than I realized because I was pleasantly surprised to learn some interesting facts that I’d missed in the Siri Recap, like “Opening a phone 20 times daily over 10 years equals 73,000 folds” or that the “machine runs approximately 22,560 cycles every 24 hours”.

But Siri’s batting average wasn’t always that good, which made it challenging to trust the notes. During a conversation with another mom about car-pool logistics, Siri Recap pulled out action items, like who I was picking up and at what time, which I appreciated, but the information wasn’t accurate. Not only had Siri gotten the names of the kids wrong, it also had me picking up the wrong kid. Clearly, the mental load of figuring out after-school logistics is challenging even for Siri.
Siri can’t handle the messy conversations (and TV shows)
Where things get interesting (and occasionally hilarious) is how Siri discerns what constitutes a conversation and how many topics belong in a single recap.

Siri is generally good at accurately labeling what conversations are about: “Parent-teacher conferences,” “Car-pool logistics,” “Folding phone durability testing.” But rather than keeping them separate, as it should, it sometimes conflates two or even three completely unrelated conversations into a single recap.

I encountered bullet points summarizing a serious conversation with a friend about a medical condition alongside notes about a chaotic (albeit funny) exploding apple cider incident with my kids. The two conversations happened within the same two-hour window, but they were by no means back-to-back.
Siri’s version:
- Details about medical condition
- Entire case of apple cider ruined after repeated warnings to stop shaking
- No more apple cider will be brought into the house
- Any remaining stickiness on the floor results in no iPad on the plane
It’s a good thing Siri Recap leaves out tone and volume cause that last bullet would’ve been in ALL CAPS.

What it did decide was worthy of a standalone recap was a discussion about wedding plans during an episode of Nobody Wants This on Netflix. To be fair, this would’ve absolutely warranted a recap if I’d been discussing my own wedding plans; however, the fact that the “conversation” happened at midnight should’ve tipped off Siri that this was a late-night binge session and not an actual conversation needing to be recapped.

Rather than coming away better informed about the important conversations I’d had throughout the day, I came away feeling validated by the sheer chaos of it all. The constant whiplash of being pulled in a dozen different directions — bouncing between work, kids, gossip and the occasional sticky beverage crisis — was real and now immortalized (until the recap automatically expires if you don’t choose to save it).
A case for manually enabling Siri Recap during meetings

For now, while novel, neither Siri Recap nor Live Rewind is reason enough to buy (or avoid) the Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4. They’re two of our top-rated smartwatches for their fitness, health and other smart features. Audio Intelligence is either an added bonus (it’s free) or something you can ignore altogether.
But if you do decide to venture into this brave new world of AI notetakers, my suggestion would be to use Siri Recap intentionally rather than leaving it running all day.

Turn it on before a work meeting, a doctor’s appointment or another conversation where you might want a few notes to jog your memory later. Just make sure everyone involved knows it’s enabled and is comfortable with it, and that you’re not relying on it for crucial information.
If the stakes are high, have a backup — whether that’s your own notes or a recording — lest you risk coming home with the wrong kid.

articles.headline: Preventing campus sexual assault could start in kindergarten
keyFacts: Experts argue that preventing campus sexual assault requires comprehensive sex education starting in kindergarten rather than relying solely on punishment and enforcement.
Comprehensive sex education teaches students boundary setting, communication, and mutual desire, which studies suggest lowers the risk of later sexual assault.
Despite bipartisan public support, comprehensive sex education mandates frequently face political opposition and legislative roadblocks in states and at the federal level.
body: The campus of Cornell University on September 30, soon after the New York attorney general announced a review of the school’s handling of assault allegations. | Spencer Platt/Getty Images

In the weeks since Jane Doe alleged she was gang-raped at a Cornell University fraternity party in 2024, the plague of campus sexual assault has once again become the topic of a heated national debate.

Those discussions inevitably land on familiar solutions. Experts, pundits, and parents argue for stricter criminal laws and a more transparent and punitive Title IX campus adjudicatory process. But these solutions have been tried in the past and not proven effective: Campus climate surveys show persistently high rates of assault, and Cornell’s own data show that reported incidents rose from 23 percent to 35 percent between 2023 and 2025.

It’s increasingly clear that to make meaningful progress requires a focus on prevention — not just punishment. Anyone horrified by the Cornell fraternity text thread published by the New York Times would agree that enforcement is only part of the story, and a fuller solution would begin with raising young people who don’t think it is remotely okay to treat each other’s bodies and emotions this way. There is a group of scholars and advocates across the country who are working on one surprisingly effective policy that might get us closer to that goal: comprehensive sex education.

Yes, you read that right: sex ed. But not sex ed as it’s currently taught in most American public schools — a haphazard set of state programs, often deeply political, which often stress abstinence over how to be in healthy sexual relationships with other people. This other version, known as comprehensive sex ed and currently required in just seven states , takes a holistic approach with focus on how to refuse unwanted sexual advances, establish clear boundaries, and have intimate relationships based on open communication and mutual desire, not force, coercion, or extreme intoxication.

An important step in the prevention of sexual assault is making comprehensive sex ed more common in American schools, and, in the states that do, making that education start earlier and comply with the National Sex Education Standards . Evidence suggests that this kind of instruction can reduce sexual violence.

Giving young people information about contraception and how to avoid STIs is an essential part of sex ed, but it isn’t enough. Far too many of our children head off to college without the interpersonal skills required to have healthy relationships involving physical intimacy, which are critical to their psychological development into caring and fulfilled adults.

The consequences can be devastating, and I see them firsthand. I am a law professor who runs a clinical program at the University of San Francisco that trains second- and third-year law students by having them litigate real cases under close supervision. Since 2018, we have been representing Title IX clients — the accusers and those they accuse — at colleges and universities all over the United States. In every case, every time, the end result is the same: pain, heartbreak, and ruined lives. The legal “resolution” is almost beside the point.

The allegations in the Cornell case are at the extreme end of the spectrum. In nearly all of the cases we handle, there is no malicious intent or casual cruelty. Instead, there are two young people who are inexperienced, hesitant to convey their real feelings, and bad at reading nonverbal cues. They drink excessively and use drugs to overcome their awkwardness and insecurity, which only makes the poor communication worse. My colleague and I joke bleakly that we are in the wrong business. What we really need to be doing is going to secondary schools and preaching the value of comprehensive sex ed to tweens and teens to stop these assaults from happening in the first place.

Recently, I interviewed Jennifer Hirsch, who is a professor at Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health and the co-author with Princeton sociologist Shamus Khan of the book Sexual Citizens , which synthesizes the findings of a five-year study of campus sexual assault that surveyed 2,000 students attending Columbia and Barnard.
“Thinking ambitiously about prevention requires that we get some more tools in the toolbox.”
Jennifer Hirsch, Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health

Sex education needs to start in kindergarten, she said, by teaching children to respect the bodies of their classmates by keeping their hands to themselves and refraining from playground activities like chasing down a classmate trying to kiss them. In higher grades, she explained, the instruction should change to become more age-appropriate, gradually adding topics relating to sexual health for tweens and teens “to teach the things you need to know, to grow into being a person who can have sex without hurting other people or yourself.” Currently, only Washington and Oregon start this early. (A few other states begin in first grade.)

While it is true that many colleges and universities have mandatory trainings for students that involve learning about consent, bystander intervention, and how intoxication is a risk factor for sexual assault, it is too little, too late. By then, Hirsch said, “there is a non-trivial possibility that they’ve already experienced sexual violence or perpetrated sexual violence.” She compared it to “starting with calculus when they’ve never done arithmetic.”

The need for such education is even more urgent today when kids snap and text instead of talk face-to-face as they are fed a diet of toxic social media messages and violent pornography that tells them what women want is to be dominated, degraded, and objectified.

Gen Z in particular is in desperate need of a sexual education that is designed to dispel the fear, shame, and ignorance most young people feel around this topic and replace it with candid instruction on how to set boundaries, read cues, and treat intimate partners — whether it is a long-term relationship or a casual hook-up — with a basic modicum of respect and care.

Study after study has shown that there is widespread bipartisan support for having sex ed incorporated into secondary school instruction that teaches students the skills they need to have safe and healthy sexual relationships. Comprehensive sex education holds promise in combatting sexual assault, although the data is limited. A 2016 survey of more than 1,600 college students led by John Santelli, who is also a professor at Columbia’s Mailman School (and Hirsch’s spouse) found that when high schoolers received comprehensive sex education, it lowered their risk of sexual assault in college. Instruction stressing abstinence or how to avoid unwanted pregnancies and STIs did not.

This makes intuitive sense. If a young person learns early on how to extricate themselves from a sexual encounter that has turned uncomfortable or scary, they will be more likely to leave before an assault happens. If he or she is taught that other people’s bodies are not theirs for the taking, they will be less likely to violate them and instead ask for clarity whenever there is ambiguity about consent.

Still most schools shy away from such instruction. “It is better to tell kids that rape is bad than to say nothing,” but to stop there and hope for the best is not effective, Hirsch told me. “Thinking ambitiously about prevention requires that we get some more tools in the toolbox.”

But comprehensive sex ed, despite its popularity, has for decades been blocked by a minority of loud opposition, often motivated by religious beliefs , in states that consider adopting it. Since 2017 , New York state lawmakers have advocated for a law mandating comprehensive sex ed for students in grades K-12. Every year, Hirsch told me, it dies in committee. At the federal level, the Trump administration has eliminated most of the federal grant money for sex ed that isn’t abstinence-only even though the research has shown that telling kids to “just say no” to sex has no impact on their behavior.

Suspension, expulsion, even criminal prosecution are not the solutions. They are the inadequate answers on offer by the adults in the room, who are trained only to react once the problem has become too big and ugly to ignore in any particular case before bracing for the next one. Reducing the accused to monsters and the accuser to a pitiable victim reinfects the wound, it does nothing to heal it. Wringing one’s hands and asking why, a generation later nothing has changed, virtually guarantees that nothing ever will.
If we really want to combat the plague of sexual assault on campus, we need to vaccinate our children in the same way we would against a lethal virus. Comprehensive sex ed is the best place to start.

articles.headline: Microsoft's school email bill gives rivals something to smile about
keyFacts: Microsoft announced education price increases and service cuts, retiring free student email and collaboration services.
The UK Department for Education expressed disappointment, as institutions face new recurring bills for previously free features.
Rivals stated that affected institutions have time to plan and migrate to alternative software options before changes begin in 2028.
body: The fallout from Microsoft's education price rises and service cuts continues as institutions weigh the prospect of bigger bills, and the Windows maker's rivals struggle not to pull "I told you so" faces.

The main takeaways are that free student email and collaboration services are being retired, and storage entitlements are changing. These changes generally apply at institutions' first renewal or extension on or after January 1, 2028. Microsoft announced the new plans last week, and the UK's Department for Education described itself as "disappointed" at the news.
As well it might be, although the UK government has rarely seen a deal from Microsoft that it didn't like . Or, for that matter, other US tech giants .

Exactly how much educational institutions will have to spend remains unclear. Mary Jo Foley of Directions on Microsoft put indicative student pricing at $2 per year for Microsoft 365 Education A2, $4 for A3, and $6 for A5, with Teams adding another dollar annually. Faculty licenses cost considerably more, while the new A7 student tier jumps to $385 a year before Teams. Foley cautioned that these were approximate figures, with actual prices set by Microsoft's partners.

The new no-cost student tier, Microsoft 365 Education A0, is a poor replacement for Office 365 A1: it excludes Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Teams. Eligibility also requires full paid faculty coverage on A2 or higher and students who actively use Windows devices for education – potentially awkward for institutions running fleets of Chromebooks.
A few dollars per student might not sound alarming. Multiply that across an institution, however, and something that used to be free becomes a recurring bill.

Michael Meeks, CEO of Collabora Productivity, told The Register: "Free was the bait on the hook, and Microsoft spent years reeling in schools' email accounts, documents, identity management and classrooms onto its cloud."
A poster on the edugeek.net forums commented: "This was always going to happen, I remember thinking this when we moved over to the MS free cloud solution. It will be free until they decide it isn't."

The risk for Microsoft is that there are options. Meeks told us: "Schools now have a year to plan, and, in our experience with other large-scale educational projects, such as the University of Lille, that can be enough time to migrate properly."

Other options include Nextcloud, which will be rolled out as part of Germany's Educational Cloud Infrastructure . Several Swiss universities also migrated to the service over an August weekend. According to Nextcloud, 39,500 students, teachers, and researchers, along with 585 terabytes of data, were shifted.
Both Nextcloud and Collabora Productivity also highlight another factor that could drive educational institutions away from Microsoft: sovereignty.

Dr Patrick Alberts, managing director of messaging provider Element, told The Register : "When an organization is locked to a vendor, it should be no surprise when that vendor takes advantage. When switching is made difficult, the vendor holds all the leverage. They can raise prices or slash services on a whim, knowing customers will swallow the pain rather than rip out the infrastructure.
"Yet it's a bold move, given European governments are proactively following a digitally sovereign strategy."

Switching suppliers still takes planning, and the alternatives won't necessarily replace every Microsoft service. But the Windows behemoth has given educational institutions a fresh reason to investigate – and its rivals a particularly convenient opening pitch. ®
